description:
Flagler County has been under a declared state of local emergency due to Hurricane Matthew since October 4, 2016. During that time, other storms have struck the County exacerbating the damage to the dune system and compounding the exposure of public and private property on the barrier island to future storms and flooding. The County also declared local states of emergency for Hurricane Irma (2017), Hurricane Dorian (2019), Hurricane Isaias (2020), and Hurricanes Ian and Nicole (2022).
Due to the cumulative effect of the storms as well as tidal events, nor’easters, and erosion, Flagler County continues to be in the most precarious position relative to ocean flooding and storms in its history. Although the County has completed a series of emergency protective berm projects since Hurricane Matthew, public and private property on the barrier island remain vulnerable to catastrophic storm damage without further and sustained protective efforts.
As part of addressing the emergency, the Board adopted a long-term beach management plan assisted by an independent coastal engineer, the County’s engineering staff and with input from residents and local HOAs. Continuing the state of local emergency will help the County with its ongoing and future efforts and allow the County to take any necessary emergency measures, including expedited emergency procurement and the issuance of emergency administrative orders, as necessary.
title: Ratification and Approval of Proclamations Extending the Local State of Emergency Due to Severe Coastal Erosion and Vulnerability.

description:
Staff is seeking approval of a budget transfer from General Fund Restricted Reserves and the approval of Work Authorization 2 (WA-2) for consulting services to complete the design and permitting phase of the Malacompra Canal Restoration and Resilience project.
On April 1, 2024, the Board approved to adopt the Stormwater Master Plan (SMP) and to obligate $2,289,108.00 of ARPA funding toward the implementation of the SMP top five (5) Stormwater Capital Improvement Projects. The Malacompra Road Canal Restoration and Resilience project was one of the listed and approved SMP priority projects. In a following regular meeting on December 2, 2024, the Board approved Work Authorization No. 012Q-WA-14 under Request for Statement of Qualifications (RSQ) 21-012Q to England-Thims & Miller (ETM) in the Amount of $495,000 utilizing ARPA funding for the design and permitting of the Malacompra Canal Restoration and Resilience Project. ARPA funding expires on December 31, 2026, and any qualifying billing activity for the Malacompra Canal Restoration and Resilience project that is to be reimbursed through the program will require completed payment processing by the end of the year deadline. As of October 31st, 2026, the consultant has billed a total of $404,303.45 for the design and permitting services. Since the project permitting phase will not be completed until summer of 2027, ARPA funding will not be available to cover the remaining project balance. General fund restricted reserves from the Hammock Dunes CDD DRI are available for use toward eligible Malacompra canal infrastructure improvements.
Staff is requesting a budget transfer of $90,697 from restricted General Fund Reserves for the purposes of completing the Malacompra Canal drainage improvements associated with the project near A1A and Bings Landing to cover the difference of the ARPA shortfall.
Additionally, during the course of the Malacompra Canal Restoration and Resilience project design and permitting development, the County received comments from the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) on behalf of the Florida Communities Trust (FCT). A portion of the Malacompra Canal Restoration and Improvements project is located on a portion of the property that has limiting conditions of use and development. The FDEP is requiring the County to perform a Cultural Resources Assessment Survey (CRAS) within a limited area of the project limits to meet the conditions of the deed restrictions. A Work Authorization has been developed under Continuing Contract for Professional Services 25-RFP-039 with Terracon Consultants, Inc. to complete the additional required CRAS services for the Not to Exceed (NTE) amount of $9,950.
title: Approval of Malacompra Canal Restoration and Resilience Project Budget Transfer and CRAS Work Authorization.

description:
This item was previously considered at the Board's November 9, 2026 workshop meeting. At the workshop meeting, the Board requested that staff provide a draft agreement for its review at today's regular Board meeting.
Due to the limited time between the two meetings, County staff prepared a revised Agreement that constitutes a complete rewrite of the previous Agreement. In the proposed FY 2026-27 Agreement, funding is limited to $350,000 per year payable to the Flagler Humane Society (FHS) in equal monthly installments of $29,166.67, retroactive to October 1, 2026. Services provided by FHS to the County are divided into Mandatory Services (limited to those required by statute or by code, and including sheltering related to local emergencies) and Additional Services (primarily the sheltering of strays). A section was added by County staff that allows for FHS to request assistance from the Board for any extraordinary circumstances that occur, with the number of animals constituting an extraordinary circumstance changed from five or more animals to 25 or more animals.
As can be expected, the passage of Amendment 3 substantially changes our approach towards this Agreement. County staff contends that this Agreement far exceeds the equivalent share of the funding support provided to FHS by our municipal partners: we continue to fund the bulk of FHS operations through this Agreement. As proposed, Mandatory Services are limited to the required activities and should stay well-below the annual funding provided through this Agreement, while any excess funds (up to the $350,000 annual funding provided) can be used by FHS to provide the Additional Services that are part of the FHS mission and scope, but are not statutory or code requirements for the County to provide or fund. As the County prepares its FY 2027-28 budget, further service level cuts are likely, as well as another shift in the County's approach towards meeting its statutory and code obligations to provide core animal control services.
title: Consideration of FY 2026-27 Agreement with the Flagler Humane Society for Animal Control Services.

2026 11 02 Emergency Proclamation - Extending LSE - Hurricane Matthew, Ian & Nicole

description:
Flagler County has been under a declared state of local emergency due to Hurricane Matthew since October 4, 2016. During that time, other storms have struck the County exacerbating the damage to the dune system and compounding the exposure of public and private property on the barrier island to future storms and flooding. The County also declared local states of emergency for Hurricane Irma (2017), Hurricane Dorian (2019), Hurricane Isaias (2020), and Hurricanes Ian and Nicole (2022).
Due to the cumulative effect of the storms as well as tidal events, nor’easters, and erosion, Flagler County continues to be in the most precarious position relative to ocean flooding and storms in its history. Although the County has completed a series of emergency protective berm projects since Hurricane Matthew, public and private property on the barrier island remain vulnerable to catastrophic storm damage without further and sustained protective efforts.
As part of addressing the emergency, the Board adopted a long-term beach management plan assisted by an independent coastal engineer, the County’s engineering staff and with input from residents and local HOAs. Continuing the state of local emergency will help the County with its ongoing and future efforts and allow the County to take any necessary emergency measures, including expedited emergency procurement and the issuance of emergency orders, as necessary.
title: Ratification and Approval of Proclamations Extending the Local State of Emergency Due to Severe Coastal Erosion and Vulnerability.

attachments.name: Flagler County BOCC Subrecipient Agreement BB205

description:
On July 15, 2024, the Board of County Commissioners approved a grant agreement with the Department of Economic Opportunity, Office of Broadband for the Multi-Purpose Community Facilities (MPCF) Program. The primary objective of the MPCF Program is to provide funds to subrecipients for the construction of, or improvements to, facilities designed to jointly and directly enable work, education, and health monitoring, located in eligible communities with an identified critical need for the project. The County used the funds to construct the Nexus Center, which includes the Bunnell Branch Library and Administrative Headquarters, the Health and Human Services Department, and the Community Center.
The grant agreement is now scheduled for close out. RSM US LLP, the contractor servicing the grant agreement, has indicated that one outstanding item needed for successful close-out is a covenant of use. The contractor has pointed to Section 11 (Ownership and Disposition of Project Property) of Exhibit A (Scope of Work) to the grant agreement. Specifically, Section 11.d. of Exhibit A refers to only a portion of 2 C.F.R. 200.316 in providing that "[p]ursuant to 2 C.F.R. 200.316, for the duration of the Federal Interest Period, the Subrecipient must hold Agreement Property in trust for the beneficiaries of this broadband infrastructure project." Section 11.c. of Exhibit A further provides that the Federal Interest Period lasts until December 31, 2034. Nowhere, however, does the grant agreement or any of its exhibits require the recording of a covenant of use.
Rather, the contractor has cited to 2 C.F.R. 200.316 in its entirety (including a portion not included in the grant agreement), which reads as follows:
Real property, equipment, and intangible property acquired or improved with the Federal award must be held in trust by the recipient or subrecipient as trustee for the beneficiaries of the project or program under which the property was acquired or improved. The Federal agency or pass-through entity may require the recipient or subrecipient to record liens or other appropriate notices of record to indicate that personal or real property has been acquired or improved with a Federal award and that use and disposition conditions apply to the property. (Emphasis added.)
As it explicitly states, a Federal agency or pass-through entity may require the recordation of a document of record. Absent such a requirement in the grant agreement itself, staff is asking the Board of County Commissioners to approve the covenant of use drafted for this purpose. The covenant of use, as drafted, simply provides as follows:
The Property Owner further agrees that this restriction shall be deemed a covenant running with the land, and shall remain in full force and effect, and be binding upon the undersigned, their heirs and assigns, from the date of recording of this Covenant in the Public Records of Flagler County until December 31, 2034, unless Property Owner receives direction from Commerce that the Covenant can be released prior to the expiration of the federal use period, as defined in the Award Documentation. This Covenant shall automatically expire at 11:59 PM on December 31, 2034 without further action being required by the Property Owner to remove the Covenant from the Property.
It is important to note that it will only be effective until December 31, 2034, the end of the Federal Interest Period, at which time it will expire on its own terms. This is a far less onerous encumbrance than it could be, as we are told by the contractor that the Federal Interest Period is typically 39.5 years. The covenant of use will be in place for just over 8 years.
title: Approval of Covenant of Use Relative to Nexus Center Use as a Multi-Purpose Community Facility.

attachments.name: DRAFT Flagler Palm Coast 2026 2028 LHAP  Manufactured Housing and Purchase Asst Amnd (redline)

description:
The Florida Housing Finance Corporation administers the State Housing Initiatives Partnership program (SHIP), which provides funds to local governments as an incentive to create partnerships that produce and preserve affordable homeownership and multifamily housing. The program is designed to serve very low, low, and moderate income families. SHIP funds are distributed to all 67 counties and 55 cities in Florida. The minimum allocation is $350,000 per county. In order to participate, local governments must establish a local housing assistance program and a local housing assistance plan (LHAP).
Flagler County administers SHIP, in partnership with City of Palm Coast. The SHIP statute allows funding of a variety of activities aimed at preserving and increasing the availability of affordable housing opportunities. Activities must align with Rule 67-37 F.A.C. including income eligibility, affordability periods, and monitoring requirements. Activities are required to be codified in the LHAP (Local Housing Assistance Plan), a mandatory County, City, and state-approved document that outlines how Flagler will spend SHIP funds over a three‑year period.
The proposed amendment to the previously approved 2026-2028 LHAP would expand the purchase/down payment assistance to more eligible first-time homebuyers, beyond the previously limited priority population of public employees and essential workers, to now serve all eligible households in the County. The current LHAP limits eligibility to this state-defined population, whereas the proposed amendment still allows their prioritization, but also expands eligibility to the broader population.
Staff also seeks approval to scale back the newly added resale and shared equity restrictions implemented in the current LHAP, to allow a 3-month period to meet current, stricter, resale limitations to a qualifying SHIP Purchase Assistance-approved household, then revert to the more traditional resale and loan repayment requirements for the remainder of the loan term. Both the current restrictions on program eligibility and resale, while originally well intended, are expected to negatively hinder program operations and timely expenditure of state funds.
Finally, the proposed amendment adds a new statutorily required program component to support Manufactured Housing. Prior statutes limited support for such homes, but new state regulations have established respective program parameters now required in the amended LHAP, allowing rehabilitation and purchase of certain manufactured housing as an eligible activity under SHIP.
The Palm Coast City Council reviewed and approved these LHAP amendments at their October 20, 2026 meeting. One proposed LHAP amendment, allowing funding for affordable rental development projects, was not approved by the Council for inclusion in these changes.
The proposed changes are intended to provide greater flexibility in addressing local housing needs while also maintaining compliance with SHIP programmatic and statutory requirements. The proposed amendments will help expand affordable housing opportunities, support homeownership, and provide additional resources for eligible Palm Coast residents.
title: Approval of Amendments to Flagler County/Palm Coast State Housing Initiative Partnership Program's Local Housing Assistance Plan, Updating Purchase Assistance Program and Adding Manufactured Housing Program Components.

attachments.name: 3 Year Contract- 2025 04 21 Agmt - NeoGov Q-368280 HR Software (7h)

description:
On April 21, 2025, the Board approved a three-year contract with NeoGov to provide four additional software modules at a total cost of $177,477.64 for the three-year term.
The approved modules included:
Learn – A countywide learning management system used to create, deliver, and track employee training.
Perform – A performance management system used to conduct employee evaluations and monitor performance throughout the year.
Onboard – A module designed to digitize and streamline the employee onboarding process.
EForms – A module used to create a digital employee filing system and digitize commonly used forms.
Prior to this approval, the County utilized two NeoGov modules that provided a digital applicant tracking and management system. These modules have been in use since 2018 with a current annual cost of $17,025.36.
In 2025, 911 Dispatch Operations transitioned from the Sheriff's Office to the County. As part of that transition, the County committed to ensuring the department maintained its required certifications. The certification process requires the use of a policy management system. NeoGov's PowerPolicy module provides this functionality for Dispatch Operations at an annual cost of $8,231.64.
Because these additional modules are provided by the same vendor, staff determined that it was appropriate to seek Board approval for the related contracts. The costs associated with these modules have already been incorporated into the FY 2026-2027 approved budget.
(Added 10.28.2026) As it relates to the contract terms, it is important to note that the original NeoGov contract provides that the contract shall be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of the County's state (Florida). The proposed contracts associated with the additional modules, conversely, provide that the contracts shall be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of the state of California. They further provide that any legal action or proceeding relating to the contracts shall be instituted only in any state or federal court in Los Angeles, California. We bring this to your attention because breach of contract claims are typically not covered by insurance and, as such, the County would likely have to retain special counsel, at its cost, to represent its interests in California.
title: Approval of FY 2026-27 NeoGov Contract.

description:
The Board previously discussed its Agreement renewal with the Flagler Humane Society (FHS) as part of its September 14, 2026 Workshop Meeting. At the Workshop Meeting, the Board requested that staff request either a 30- or 60-day extension from the Flagler Humane Society: a 20-day extension until October 20, 2026 was ultimately granted. As of the date of this meeting, there is no active agreement between the County and the FHS.
Under the FY 2025-26 Agreement, a total of $106,000 was allocated for Animal Shelter Services and the Spay and Neuter Program (Section 2.b. from the Agreement). The Agreement calls for spending reaching 90% of the total ($95,400) to prompt notification: as of the end of April’s invoices, spending was at $86,856 (81.9%) and by the end of May, total spending for the year had increased to $101,231 (95.5%). The total contracted amount remained at $320,599. An amendment to the Agreement (Amendment No. 1) was approved on August 14, 2026, increasing the contracted total to $352,658.90, a $32,059.90 (10%) increase. By the end of September, combined spending for the Animal Shelter Services and the Spay and Neuter Program had reached $159,022 where only $106,000 had been initially budgeted per the Agreement, resulting in a shortfall of $20,962.10 after the Amendment No. 1 10% increase amount was included. Funding in the amount of $20,962.10 will be transferred from General Fund 1001 Reserves to make up for the immediate shortfall.
A Third Amendment (Amendment No. 3) to the FY 2025-26 Agreement is needed to cover the overage, bringing the total compensation amount to $373,621 for the FY 2025-26 Agreement. While Amendment No. 1 increased the available funds, Amendment No. 2 (effective September 28, 2026) extended the FY 2025-26 Agreement through October 20, 2026. Amendment No. 3 would be retroactive to October 20, 2026, and would: (1) extend the FY 2025-26 Agreement from October 20, 2026 to November 2, 2026; and (2) modify the total contract cost from $352,658.90 to $373,621.00 to cover the shortfall amount.
The County is seeking an amended Agreement centering on the required elements from Florida Statutes and the County's Code of Ordinances: dangerous dogs; custodial care (for example, when an animal is impounded because of the arrest of the owner); and animal abuse and neglect. As drafted, this Agreement requires that FHS seek reimbursement for its costs from an animal owner first before billing sheltering costs to the County. Labor costs - the cost of the Animal Control Officer - are reimbursable by the County on an hourly basis when conducting the County's contracted activities; however, any medical costs would not be reimbursed. This iteration of the Agreement also provides that the County may revoke the appointment of Animal Control Officers, or the County may hire its own Officers. In addition, the Humane Society is required to report to the County any complaints and how they are resolved. This is a shift in the funded activities that the County's contract with FHS had previously provided. This does not mean that FHS should not provide services that are not included in the Agreement with the County; however, it does limit the County's funding of FHS to the essential services required by Florida Statutes and the County's Code of Ordinances.
title: Consideration of Approval of: a Budget Transfer in the Amount of $20,963; a Contract Amendment to Extend the Contract Term and Increase the Contract Amount; and the Animal Control Services Contract for FY 2026-27 with Flagler County Humane Society.

description:
As the construction of the new Fire Station 51 on County Road 305 nears completion, the future use or disposal of the current Fire Station 51 site at 3055 County Road 13 can now be determined. Section 125.35, Florida Statutes, authorizes the County to sell and convey any real or personal property, and to lease real property belonging to the county, whenever the board determines that it is to the best interest of the county to do so, to the highest and best bidder for the particular use the board deems to be the highest and best, for such length of term and such conditions as the governing body may in its discretion determine.
The subject parcel (Parcel No. 31-11-30-0000-01050-0020) is described as having dimensions of 83.82 feet by 375.00 feet (31,452.5 s.f.; 0.72 acres), and is described in its conveyance documents as 0.69 acres in size:
This parcel is part of former railroad right-of-way, now vacated. The parcel was initially conveyed through a Deed of Gift dated February 25, 1988 by the Container Corporation of America to the Espanola Volunteer Fire Department, Inc., and recorded on May 20, 1988 at Official Records Book 349, Page 611, Public Records of Flagler County, Florida. The subsequent Quit-Claim Deed dated April 15, 1988 by the Espanola Volunteer Fire Department to the Flagler County Board of County Commissioners (recorded on May 20, 1988 at Official Records Book 349, Page 616, Public Records of Flagler County, Florida) conveyed the Volunteer Fire Department's interest in the parcel to the County. No covenants or restrictions were found that would prevent the conveyance or use of the subject parcel by a successor tenant or owner. The parcel is zoned MH-1 (Rural Mobile Home) District, and is a nonconforming lot of record. Current Property Appraiser records list the parcel's just (market) value at $129,018.
While substantial completion of the new Fire Station 51 will occur in the next month, it is anticipated that the Fire Department will have fully vacated the Espanola Fire Station parcel by January 31, 2027. The assumption of use by a new owner or tenant would then commence no earlier than February 1, 2027. If the Board determines that this parcel is surplus, it may be sold or leased as provided in Florida Statutes.
It should be noted that in addition to the provisions of Section 125.35, Florida Statutes, that the statutes additionally include Section 125.38, Florida Statutes, that provides a separate process for conveyance or lease to "the United States, or any department or agency thereof, the state or any political subdivision or agency thereof, or any municipality of this state, or corporation or other organization not for profit which may be organized for the purposes of promoting community interest and welfare".
title: Consideration of Determination of Surplus Land and Solicitation for Sale or Lease to Highest and Best Bidder - Fire Station 51, 3055 County Road 13, Bunnell.

description:
The original ordinance governing the provision of emergency medical services (EMS) within Flagler County, addressing agencies licensed for basic life support (BLS) or advanced life support (ALS) by the State of Florida, was established in 1991.
The current ordinance has established a process for public or private entities desiring to provide EMS within the County to apply for a Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity (COPCN) through an advisory board. However, criteria to apply for a COPCN by an interested provider contains requirements that have proven to be unachievable. As a result, entities desiring to obtain a COPCN to serve Flagler County cannot make application to the EMS Advisory Board for consideration.
Following the issuance of recent COPCNs, the Emergency Medical Services Advisory Board (EMSAB) recommended an update of the current ordinance to maintain an effective, high-quality EMS delivery system for residents and visitors. The proposed amended and restated ordinance establishes clear application requirements and ensures the EMSAB can evaluate any applicants for a COPCN within Flagler County.

description:
As provided in Section 212.055(3), Florida Statutes, Florida counties having a total population of 50,000 or less on April 1, 1992, are eligible to levy the Small County Surtax at the rate of 0.5 or 1 percent. Flagler County is one of thirty-one counties eligible to levy the Small County Surtax, but the only one of the thirty-one to levy the tax at 0.5 percent; the remaining thirty counties levy the tax at the full 1 percent. In 2012 the County adopted Ordinance 2012-08, levying the Small County Surtax at a rate of 0.5 percent throughout the County (referenced in the attached ordinance imposing the "Second Small County Surtax" as the "First Half Cent Sales Tax"). The First Half Cent Sales Tax took effect on January 1, 2013 and was approved for a period of 20 years, expiring on December 31, 2032 unless renewed or otherwise extended. The proceeds of the First Half Cent Sales Tax are utilized by the County and its municipalities for the construction or improvement of public facilities, as well as the operational expenses of any infrastructure as that term is defined by Section 212.055(3)(d)2., Florida Statutes, and for any other public purpose authorized by Section 212.055(3)(d)1., Florida Statutes.
Proceeds of the Small County Surtax may be distributed through one of two possible methods:An interlocal agreement approved by the county’s governing body and the governing bodies of the municipalities representing a majority of the county’s municipal population. This agreement may include a school district with the consent of all governing bodies previously mentioned.
If there is no interlocal agreement, then the distribution will be based on the Local Government Half-cent Sales Tax formulas provided in s. 218.62, F.S.
Proceeds and accrued interest can be used for:Servicing bonded indebtedness to finance, plan, and construct infrastructure and acquiring land for public recreation, conservation, or protection of natural resources, where infrastructure means any fixed capital expenditure or cost associated with the construction, reconstruction, or improvement of public facilities having a life expectancy of 5 or more years and any related land acquisition, land improvement, design, and engineering costs; or
Operational expenses of any infrastructure or any public purpose authorized in the ordinance.
Use of the Small County Surtax proceeds for bonded indebtedness requires voter approval in a countywide referendum, while use of proceeds for operational expenses of any infrastructure or any public purpose authorized in the ordinance requires an extraordinary (supermajority of four or more Commissioners voting in favor) vote of the Board of County Commissioners.
Based on the 2025 Local Government Financial Information Handbook (the "2025 Handbook"), Flagler County's present tax rate of 0.5 percent resulted in an estimated $10,670,935 in countywide realized tax revenues for the local fiscal year ending September 30, 2026. Imposition of an additional 0.5 percent (one-half cent) sales tax would yield approximately $10.6 million in additional revenue, to be distributed between the county and the municipalities based on population (the same manner as the existing 0.5 percent is distributed), and for the purpose of funding operational expenses of any infrastructure or any public purpose authorized in the ordinance imposing the additional tax.
Based on the 2025 Handbook, the 1 percent distribution would be as provided in the middle column below, with the estimated distribution amount (as of September 30, 2026) in the right column:
As provided in the ordinance imposing the Second Small County Surtax (attached):
"The County and its municipalities continue to have infrastructure needs which cannot be met with existing revenue sources. The County needs additional funding for its Capital Improvement Plan, Road & Bridge Maintenance Program, Beach Management Plan, Stormwater Master Plan, Pavement Resurfacing Policy, maintenance of County buildings, and management of conservation areas."
This surtax is one of several surtaxes subject to a combined rate limitation. A county cannot levy this surtax and the Small County Surtax, Indigent Care and Trauma Center Surtax, and County Public Hospital Surtax in excess of a combined rate of 1 percent. If approved, the Second Small County Surtax levying the additional 0.5 percent sales tax will not go into effect until January 1, 2028.

Although the County has completed a series of emergency protective berm projects since Hurricane Matthew, public and private property on the barrier island remain vulnerable to catastrophic storm damage without further and sustained protective efforts.
As part of addressing the emergency, the Board adopted a long-term beach management plan assisted by an independent coastal engineer, the County’s engineering staff and with input from residents and local HOAs. Continuing the state of local emergency will help the County with its ongoing and future efforts and allow the County to take any necessary emergency measures, including expedited emergency procurement and the issuance of emergency administrative orders, as necessary.
title: Ratification and Approval of Proclamations Extending the Local State of Emergency Due to Severe Coastal Erosion and Vulnerability.

description:
The parcel owners of 3936 Evergreen Avenue contacted County staff several months ago about donating this parcel to the County. The subject parcel is located at the north-east corner of the intersection of Forest Park Street and Evergreen Avenue, with 400 feet of frontage along Forest Park Street and 120 feet of frontage along Evergreen Avenue (dimensions of 400 feet by 120 feet) and a parcel area of 48,000 square feet (1.10 acres). The property is being offered to Flagler County as a free transfer. The property is being offered because the owners feel that the subject parcel has low development potential. The vacant property is located on the north side of Evergreen Avenue, east of Forest Park Street and west of County Road 305, and is more specifically described as Lot 35, Block 139, Daytona North Subdivision, as recorded in Map Book 10, Pages 1-15, Public Records of Flagler County, Florida:
This area of Daytona North is part of the western limit of Quigley Bay, and the southwesterly extension of the Big Branch Swamp draining from the north-east to the Southwest and eventually draining into Dead Lake and Crescent Lake. The subject parcel consists of Hicoria, Riviera, and Gator soils, which are listed as depressional soil units by the United States Department of Agriculture Soil Survey of Flagler County. Depressional map units are considered stand-alone criteria for one of the State of Florida’s wetland delineation tests. The property is also located within Flood Zone A, which FEMA describes as the area subject to inundation by the 1-percent-annual-chance flood event.
The Property Appraiser has recently revised the assessed value of this parcel (and others nearby) to a $250 taxable valuation. The Quigley Bay wetland system’s hydrology results in parcels that are so wet they are not cost-effective to develop when wetland permitting and mitigation combined with fill and alternative septic expenses are considered. The County’s purpose in accepting this property would be as potential mitigation for some unknown future project, and to protect future buyers from over-paying for an essentially worthless parcel (the present owners purchased the subject parcel as part of a larger package of parcels purchased in May 2007). Taxes for the subject parcel are current (Receipt #0000098 for $3.30 paid on November 30, 2025 for the 2025 Annual Tax Bill). The area surrounding this parcel remains undeveloped.
To complete this transfer, Flagler County will pay minimal closing costs. Normally, closing expenses would include title report and insurance, a Phase I environmental assessment, and a survey. For this parcel, staff is recommending waiving the Phase I environmental assessment, survey, and title insurance (a review of available aerial photography depicting this parcel found no development). Staff will physically inspect this parcel prior to closing and ensure that no Recognized Environmental Conditions exist onsite. "Recognized environmental conditions" means "the presence or likely presence of any hazardous substances or petroleum products on a property under conditions that indicate an existing release, a past release, or a material threat of a release of any hazardous substances or petroleum products into structures on the property or into the ground, ground water, or surface water of the property." Staff will utilize the same legal description found on the previous deed and not carry title insurance for this parcel.
Previously, in June 2016, the County accepted a vacant property located on the north side of Apple Avenue, and in December 2017 also accepted a parcel on the south side of Apple Avenue, both lying west of County Road 305 and more specifically described as Lot 3, Block 149, and Lot 6, Block 150, respectively, within the Daytona North Subdivision, Map Book 10, Pages 1-15.

description:
The County issued a Request for Proposals seeking a qualified organization to assume operation of the Adult Day Care (ADC) program through a Change of Ownership (CHOW) process and ensure continuity of services for program participants and their families.
The ADC program provides critical services to vulnerable adults, including supervision, social engagement, supportive care, and respite for caregivers. Given the importance of these services, the County established RFP evaluation criteria designed to identify an organization with demonstrated operational experience, financial capacity, regulatory readiness, and a comprehensive plan for sustaining services following transition from County operations.
Three proposals were received and reviewed by the evaluation committee, with the top scoring applicant discussed by the board at the 9/14/26 and 10/5/26 meetings. Considering the top applicant no longer being eligible due to an increased rates request submission post bid closure, the board directed staff to revisit the remaining proposals for viability and a recommendation to the board for consideration of award, or if more appropriate closure of the ADC.
Evaluation Summary:
Following a comprehensive re-review of all submissions, staff determined none of the remaining proposals sufficiently demonstrated the qualifications, operational readiness, financial capability, services experience and programmatic capacity necessary to ensure a successful transition and long-term operation of the ADC program.
While one proposal ranked higher than the others and was considered the most viable of the submissions received at the time, the remaining proposals led to significant uncertainties regarding each applicant's ability to successfully assume operations and complete the required Change of Ownership process. The proposals contained several unresolved issues related to organizational capacity, financial sustainability, and program implementation that prevented staff from concluding that the applicant could provide a seamless and sustainable transition.
Concerns on the second ranked proposal include that it is not currently an established business entity in the state, nor a provider of comparable services, and would require extensive organizational development, staffing recruitment, licensing preparation, fund development and operational ramp-up before pursuing and assuming responsibility for ADC operations.
Additionally, the third ranked proposal was effectively materially incomplete and failed to provide information necessary for a meaningful evaluation. Deficiencies included absence of detailed financial statements and evidence of financial capacity; a lack of demonstrated experience operating adult day care; failure to provide a comprehensive service delivery model addressing all aspects of the RFP; a lack of a participant enrollment, retention, or program growth strategy; insufficient staffing and organizational background or plans; and limited information regarding regulatory compliance and transition readiness.
Collectively, these deficiencies created substantial uncertainty regarding the ability of any other respondent to successfully assume ADC operations without disruption to participants and caregivers.
Staff Analysis:
The County's foremost responsibility is to ensure delivery of safe, stable, and high-quality services to vulnerable residents. Staff determined that awarding a contract to any of the remaining respondents would introduce significant operational, financial, regulatory, and service delivery risks.
The remaining proposals presented substantially greater concern, lacked information and experience, and demonstrated limited capacity necessary to support a recommendation for award. Based on the evaluation results, staff believes that rejecting all proposals is in the best interest of the County. Given the absence of a qualified successor organization and the risks associated with transitioning operations to any of the applicants, staff recommends an orderly wind-down of services and closure of the Adult Day Care program effective December 31, 2026.
Staff will work closely with participants, caregivers, community partners, and applicable agencies to provide advance notice of the closure, facilitate referrals to available community resources, and minimize service disruptions to the extent practicable.
Closure and Transition Plan:
Subject to Board approval, staff will implement an orderly transition and closure of Adult Day Care (ADC) operations effective January 1, 2027, with the final day of program operations occurring on December 31, 2026.
Proposed Timeline:
October 2026• Board consideration of staff recommendation to reject all proposals and authorize closure of ADC operations.
• Staff initiates closure planning activities and coordinates with regulatory agencies, community partners, and interested stakeholders.
• Development of individualized transition assistance materials and community resource information for participants and caregivers.
November 1, 2026• Formal issuance of closure notices to:
o The State of Florida and all applicable licensing agencies.
o Florida Medicaid and applicable managed care organizations.
o All current program participants and their authorized representatives, guardians, or caregivers.
o Community referral partners and service providers.
• Notice date provides a minimum of sixty (60) days advance notice before the planned closure date, satisfying applicable notification requirements.
November - December 2026• Coordination with managed care plans, case managers, caregivers, and receiving providers to facilitate continuity of care.
• Wind-down of County-operated ADC activities and closure of operational, contractual, and regulatory obligations.
December 31, 2026• Final day of Adult Day Care program operations.
January 1, 2027• Adult Day Care program ceases operations.
• Completion of final regulatory notifications, provider termination activities, record retention requirements, and closeout procedures.
The scorecard from the ranking of the responses to the RFP is attached, along with each of the submittals from each of the three prospective vendors.
title: Consideration of Adult Day Care Reassessment: Adult Day Care (ADC) Operations Request for Proposals (RFP) Review and Recommendation to Reject All Proposals, Discontinuing ADC Program Operations effective December 31, 2026.

description:
This most recent discussion and consideration of the release of the Conservation Easement has been promoted by the owner of Lot 70's request for the Board to consider releasing the Easement over Lot 70 to allow for its sale as a developable lot. As previously stated to the Board over the last 20 years Lots 70 and 71 are unique within Armand Beach East in that the Conservation Easement extends over the entirety of both lots, rendering these lots unbuildable (the Restrictions and Covenants imposed through the Conservation Easement prohibit activities which disturb the ground or vegetation with the limits of the Easement). Prior release requests have been denied by prior Boards.
Due to the enforcement provisions of the Conservation Easement falling to the County to enforce, where the Conservation Easement and the platted drainage and utility easements coincide - described as typical side and lot line easements with a width of 7.5 feet on each side (yielding a total easement width of 15 feet where applicable) - stormwater maintenance has not been possible, except for emergency maintenance activities. Previous Boards - like this Board - have considered releasing the Easement on Lot 70 (and Lot 71), releasing the Easement on other impacted lots, releasing the easement along the mosquito ditch, and other similar requests, all of which have either been denied outright or delayed for further study and discussion which never took place. There are few new ideas here: the Easement has imposed a limit on development where it exists, and it has admittedly limited maintenance activities that the HOA and lot owners could complete. As others have stated specifically to the lot owners of Lots 70 and 71, the same applies throughout Armand Beach East: everyone knew what they were getting themselves into when they bought here. To the extent that Sea Colony outfalls into the mosquito canal, and to the extent that Hammock Beach Estates does the same, other lot owners and HOAs are similarly affected by these decisions. A decision by the Board to release the Conservation Easement does not obligate the County to improve or maintain (or remedy) any stormwater system. In fact, in 2010 when the County assumed maintenance over the paved roads in Arand Beach East, the County specifically did not accept the stormwater system. Should the Board determine that the County should maintain any part of the Armand Beach East Subdivision stormwater system - even if the maintenance consists of a one-time "one-and-done" effort to correct deficiencies due to deferred maintenance - there would be an initial cost estimated at $500,000, followed by an ongoing maintenance cost of a much lower magnitude but to continue on an ongoing basis in perpetuity. Formation of a Municipal Service Benefit Unit (MSBU) is a typical option where benefit (and costs) would be limited and localized.
Both the St. Johns River Water Management District and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers - to the extent that they retain specific regulatory jurisdiction over the Conservation Easement - have both determined that the continuance of the Conservation Easement is not within their purview: they are not individually or collectively responsible to enforce the Conservation Easement. They do, however, maintain jurisdiction over specific wetland permitting requirements to the extent that these requirements apply to any development activity. Ultimately any lot or parcel presently affected Conservation Easement would need to demonstrate the suitability of the lot or parcel for development through a jurisdictional wetland determination by the appropriate agency (St. Johns River Water Management District and/or U.S. Army Corps of Engineers) inclusive of any wetland mitigation that may be required by the proposed development.
The Board may opt to:
1. Release the Conservation Easement for the entirety of the Armand Beach East Subdivision, but requiring that new impervious area and structures (except for fences) be prohibited within side and rear lot lines where the current extent of the Conservation Easement extends beyond the limits of the platted side and rear lot line drainage and utility easements. Where this situation occurs, the restriction on the impervious area and structures would be limited to the lesser of: the extent of the Conservation Easement beyond the 7.5 foot wide drainage and utility easement but less that 15 feet from any side or rear lot line; or limited to 15 feet from any side or rear lot line.
2. Release the Conservation Easement for the entirety of the Armand Beach East Subdivision with no restriction.
3. Release the Conservation Easement for Lot 70 only.
4. Release the Conservation Easement only over the portion of the Easement coinciding with the mosquito ditch through the Armand Beach East Subdivision (or, alternatively, amending the Easement to allow stormwater-related maintenance to occur within the portion of the Easement coinciding with the mosquito ditch).
5. Take no action, leaving the Conservation Easement in place.
title: Consideration of Release of Conservation Easement in Armand Beach East Subdivision.

description:
Consideration of the release of the Conservation Easement in the Armand Beach East subdivision was tabled from the August 17 regular meeting for additional information. Specifically, the Board requested an overview of the overall area drainage patterns and any jurisdictional determination documentation.
A substantial file record has been attached to this agenda item, and yet more files can be provided, the bulk of which represent two specific items: the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers' file history, which for the most part represents the punitive enforcement action against Stan Rosenbaum and requiring wetland restoration and creation (and which required creation and enforcement of the Conservation Easement); and the County's previous discussions specific to the Conservation Easement, most of which relate to the request of the owners to release the Conservation Easement on Lots 70 and 71.
Attachments to this item include: the August 17 agenda item and the Board's approved minutes from this meeting; the map and legal description for the Conservation Easement (again provided for reference); a cost estimate dated August 18, 2025 for maintenance dredging of the mosquito ditch within Armand Beach East (with a then-estimated job cost of $417,120.00); historical Board records from 1994 when the Board released and relocated the Conservation Easement within specified areas; the Board's 2010 acceptance of the maintenance over the paved roadways within Armand Beach East (but not including maintenance of the stormwater system); and the complete St. Johns River Water Management District (SJRWMD) document repository for each of the three relevant Environmental Resource Permits (ERPs) -- Armand Beach East, Hammock Beach Estates, and Sea Colony -- that cover the drainage basin in this area (note that the SJRWMD files are saved in an oldest to newest document listing based on each of these three developments, inclusive of each ERP and all permit sequences).
These documents together show a southward flow of stormwater from the north in Sea Colony to the south into the former mosquito ditch through Armand Beach East (and which provides the stormwater outfall for the Hammock Beach Estates stormwater system) and into the County's ditch between Solee Road and Malacompra Road, and eventually draining into the Matanzas Canal and the Intracoastal Waterway. It is anticipated that installation of a control structure (likely a weir) at the north end of the mosquito ditch at the Armand Beach East subdivision boundary following a modification to the Sea Colony SJRWMD ERP permit -- and remedial maintenance by the Sea Colony HOA -- will resolve drainage issues in Sea Colony. Culvert pipes installed for road crossings over the mosquito ditch in Armand Beach East are more or less level. As with most stormwater systems, a backup downstream causes upstream stormwater to collect, as was the case following Hurricane Matthew in this area.
Release of the Conservation Easement -- at least where it coincides with the platted drainage and utility easements -- will allow the respective HOAs and lot owners to complete maintenance within low-lying drainage areas along side and rear lines as applicable. Up until this point and due to the Conservation Easement coinciding with the drainage (and utility) easements, routine maintenance has not been possible: the Restrictions and Covenants accompanying the Conservation Easement specifically prohibited any maintenance other than removal of invasive plant species. As was presented to the Board at its August 17 meeting, the Board may release the entirety of the Conservation Easement, or may opt to only release the portion of the Conservation Easement over the mosquito ditch, or could release only the part of the Conservation Easement over Lots 70 and 71, or some combination of any or all of these. One recent suggestion was to release the Restrictions and Covenants within the Conservation Easement, but impose a restriction that where a Conservation Easement is present on a lot on a side or rear lot line in excess of the 7.5 foot wide drainage and utility easement, that no impervious surface or structure be placed within the lesser of the extent of the Conservation Easement beyond the 7.5 foot wide drainage and utility easement or 7.5 feet beyond the drainage and utility easement, effectively restricting the Conservation Easement to no more than 15 feet on any side or rear lot line where the Conservation Easement currently exceeds these dimensions on any one lot. This would be subject to a jurisdictional wetland determination (and wetland mitigation) that would restrict lot development. The result of this is that maintenance within the drainage areas can now occur. This release does not create a maintenance obligation on the part of Flagler County.

description:
Flagler County has been under a declared state of local emergency due to Hurricane Matthew since October 4, 2016. During that time, other storms have struck the County exacerbating the damage to the dune system and compounding the exposure of public and private property on the barrier island to future storms and flooding. The County also declared local states of emergency for Hurricane Irma (2017), Hurricane Dorian (2019), Hurricane Isaias (2020), and Hurricanes Ian and Nicole (2022).
Due to the cumulative effect of the storms as well as tidal events, Nor’easters, and erosion, Flagler County continues to be in the most precarious position relative to ocean flooding and storms in its history. Although the County has completed a series of emergency protective berm projects since Hurricane Matthew, public and private property on the barrier island remain vulnerable to catastrophic storm damage without further and sustained protective efforts.
As part of addressing the emergency, the Board adopted a long-term beach management plan assisted by an independent coastal engineer, the County’s engineering staff and with input from residents and local HOAs. Continuing the state of local emergency will help the County with its ongoing and future efforts and allow the County to take any necessary emergency measures, including expedited emergency procurement and the issuance of emergency administrative orders, as necessary.

Flagler County has a Dune Maintenance Agreement with the Hammock Dunes Owners Association (HDOA) dated August 18, 2025, for the County to provide dune restoration and associated services and the HDOA to provide $570,000.00 per year to the County towards the services.
The HDOA has asked the County to permit an offshore sand source to be useable in future projects as an alternative to sand sourced from upland mines. The County and HDOA have coordinated efforts to request the attached proposal from Foth to modify the FDEP and USACE permits and the BOEM Borrow Area Lease to dredge sand from an offshore borrow area, named 3A, temporarily stockpile the sand on the northern end of Reach II, and truck the sand from the stockpile and place it on the dunes at Hammock Dunes. The 3A borrow area is the same site used by the USACE for the Flagler County Coastal Storm Risk Management Project in Flagler Beach and will be used by the County for the Reach II Beach Nourishment Project (approved August 3, 2026).
The stockpile and transport option can potentially realize substantial savings as opposed to the use of sand trucked overland from inland mines, if performed in conjunction with a nearby dredge project that is contributing to the mobilization cost for the dredge equipment.
Considering Foth provided the Coastal Engineering support to permit both the previous Hammock Dunes project and the Reach II permits, including managing the environmental and cultural resource evaluations required for regulatory approval, it is recommended that an Amendment to the Foth contract for $148,984.00 be approved to amend the scope of work and fee for Professional Services, as described in the attachment “Exhibit A”.

description:
This item was continued from the Board's September 14, 2026 regular meeting to provide an opportunity for Commissioners to perform a site visit of Therapeutic Assisted Living's current operation.
During the July 13, 2026 meeting, the Board provided staff with consensus to issue a Request for Proposals (RFP) for the operation of the David I. Siegel Adult Day Care Center (ADC) program. This was new direction in follow up to the January 12, 2026 workshop, wherein the Board provided staff with consensus to dissolve the Adult Day Care program by the end of this fiscal year on September 30, 2026. Reasons cited by the Board for the dissolution of the program were limited enrollment relative to the ongoing costs of the program, with staff noting that despite the program costs and the equivalent of the County’s subsidy of the program, the program remains significantly less expensive to the enrollee than in-home care.
Subsequently, the Commission received two public-private partnerships requests (pursuant to Sec. 255.065, Florida Statutes) to continue Adult Day Care operations. The board directed staff to issue the RFP in light of this interest. Procurement staff issued 26-RFP-022: Operation and Program Administration of the Flagler County Adult Day Care at the David I. Siegel Center on August 3, 2026, with a proposal closing date of August 24, 2026. Three interested applicants completed the mandatory bidder conference meeting and submitted eligible proposals. Applications were received from Calvin’s Care LLC; Mishpakha Inc.; and Therapeutic Assisted Living Corp.
The evaluation committee met on September 2, 2026 to rank the scored applications, with Therapeutic Assisted Living Corp. as the highest scoring bidder to move forward for Board consideration to operate the ADC. Staff will note that while the vendor ranked highest, there are nuanced differences in the program model, levels of service and related aspects from the bidder, as well as need to ramp up staffing, transition program licensure and other aspects that will take time to complete and ultimately may result in a slightly different program model than when operated by the County. This includes limited RN/LPN staffing, which is allowable under basic ADC state licensure, but may impact medical aspects of the program, such as regular medication management and levels of available medical response in an emergency.
Should the Board approve the highest scoring applicant, staff will work closely and quickly with the vendor to complete a Change of Ownership (CHOW) with the State of Florida Agency for Health Care Administration (AHCA). The CHOW process can take 60-90 days and successful completion is required for transfer of operations. If the selected applicant CHOW is not approved by AHCA, the program licensure and operations cannot be transferred. County staff will also work with the vendor to transfer Medicaid Managed Long Term Care (MLTC) contracts and patients, as well as private pay patient care over to the new vendor. Additionally, the County will complete related agreements with the vendor to memorialize logistical aspects such as facility use and other components.
To enact this measure staff will need to extend the Adult Day Care program between 60-90 days to allow the full transition of licensure ownership and also continuity of care. Three months of gap funding, spanning October 1 to December 31, 2026 have been included in the FY 2026-27 budget to account for this transition time.
One final item of note: ITT has recently released its original deed conditions and restrictions over the subject parcel. This release would allow the County to pursue additional uses of this parcel other than for provision of senior services, or alternatively would allow for the parcel to be disposed of as surplus to the highest and best bidder for redevelopment.
title: Consideration of Approval of Awarding Request for Proposals (RFP) Response from Therapeutic Assisted Living and Carry Out Operational Transition of the David I. Siegel Adult Day Care Center.

description:
Flagler County lacks a permanent shelter for those experiencing homelessness, and the issues associated with homelessness transcend political and jurisdictional boundaries. In 2020, Flagler County together with the cities of Bunnell, Palm Coast, and Flagler Beach entered into an Interlocal Agreement (ILA) to provide a Cold Weather Shelter (CWS) for those experiencing homelessness on cold nights (nights in which the temperature is predicted to drop below forty degrees Fahrenheit) to help address this situation collaboratively. Through the ILA, the compensation rate for the nonprofit vendor - Flagler County Family Assistance Center, Inc. d/b/a The Sheltering Tree - has remained the same for the past six (6) years while CWS attendance has doubled and operational costs have increased overall. The Sheltering Tree is requesting an amendment to the ILA to increase the cost-share to cover more of the operational expenses, along with other changes to update the ILA.
The amended ILA makes the following changes to the existing ILA (referred to as the First ILA):Reference to the Church on the Rock has been removed given that it has been sold and is no longer a site for the shelter. A generic reference to the facility providing the services has been inserted in its place.
Reference to those living without heat has been added to account for those who have homes but who may need to use the Cold Weather Shelter.
The cost for services has been increased from $1,000 per night to $1,500 per night, with each jurisdiction being responsible for 25% of the per-night cost, or $375 per night.
The cap on number of days charged has been removed to account for the fact that the Cold Weather Shelter may be needed more than 24 nights a year. Nonetheless, each party’s responsibility is capped at 25% of the total cost of the Cold Weather Shelter services. Staff projects not exceeding 30 nights, equating to an $11,250 contribution from each jurisdiction.
Additionally, it is important to note that the operating costs associated with the program are expected to exceed the $1,500/day reimbursement provided for in the ILA. This is due to the expense of providing materials and supplies that include bedding, food, and other programmatic items necessary to support the 20-30 nightly participants.
County staff continue to work with the vendor on the utilization of the new Fairgrounds Expo Hall as the preferred CWS location. Recently, the County and The Sheltering Tree staff conducted a walk-thru meeting at the Expo Hall, and all parties agreed that it would be a viable location for the CWS. As logistics to make this arrangement possible are addressed, staff will take the applicable steps necessary to solidify this arrangement.

description:
An appeal was filed by the Owners on August 25, 2026 related to the Planning and Development Board’s most recent variance denial for variances related to the construction of a pool, pool deck, and pump house at 3 Pelican Lane. Specifically, the Appellants’/Owners’ most recent appeal requests:
“To alleviate the hardship created by only approving a 4’ structure height and my pool pump house/shed inclosure [sic]. My application has always maintain [sic] the request of 10’ and the building plans are to build 9’7” height with 5” buffer to not exceed 10’ height. My last return zoning and planning hearing resulted in a tie to approve, a tie to disapprove and 20 minutes [illegible] to the forced [sic] to make a vote 4-2. I also present [sic] a professional opinion letter that stated very clearly that my request to codes. History 7 No’s, 8 ties [sic] 4 to 2 Jan 12, 2026. TRC, has stated height is 12’. I also stated at the zoning and planning hearing that the professional stated to me the lowest I can go is 9’3” but my 10’ height request remains.”
The appeal application cites the Planning and Development Board’s Order No. 5921-A from its August 11, 2026 regular meeting, where the Board voted 4-2 on a motion to deny on the basis that the requested variance is not the minimum relief necessary to alleviate the hardship.
This is Mr. Royer’s third appeal to the Board of County Commissioners. His first and second appeals – like this appeal – sought the elimination of the Planning and Development Board’s four-foot height limitation on the proposed pump house, with all other requested variances for the pool and pool deck’s location and a variance to exceed lot coverage all approved by the Planning Board at its February 11, 2025 regular meeting. The Planning and Development Board’s approval (vote on the motion was unanimous) stated:
“The Planning and Development Board find that all the variance criteria as listed in the guidelines at Land Development Code Section 3.07.03.E have been met and therefore approves Project No. 2024110031 for 3.49 foot rear (North) variance from the minimum required 10 foot rear setback for a pool and pool deck, a 25 foot left streetside (West) variance from the minimum required 25 foot streetside setback for a pool and pool deck, a 22- foot left streetside (West) variance from the minimum required 25- foot streetside setback for a pump house, a 0.82 percent lot coverage variance from the maximum allowed 35 percent lot coverage at 3 Pelican Lane (Parcel No. 23-11-31-5300-00000-0130), subject to the following condition:
1. The pump house is to be within the boundaries of the block wall (pool barrier) and not taller than 4 feet in height.”
This first appeal was heard by the Board of County Commissioners at its May 5, 2025 regular meeting. After considering the appeal request, the Board denied (on a unanimous vote) the appeal (as copied below from the approved meeting minutes):
“A motion was made by Commissioner Hansen to deny the appeal on the basis that the Planning and Development Board’s decision was supported by competent substantial evidence, the [sic] due process was accorded to the applicant, and the essential requirements of law, primarily the four criteria for variances within the LDC, have been observed. Seconded by Commissioner Carney. Chair Dance called the question. Motion carried unanimously.”
Unlike other land use requests, variance requests are not time-barred: a reapplication could be made at any time, and the Board’s comments from the May 5, 2025 meeting concluded with this acknowledgement (again from the minutes):
“Chair Dance noted Mr. Royer would have to re-apply, bring additional evidence, and modify his plan.”
Mr. Royer did file a subsequent variance application (Project No. 2025050043), which was ultimately denied at the Planning and Development Board’s August 12, 2025 regular meeting following a tie vote (2-2) on a motion to approve. At that time, staff determined that a tie vote results in a denial of the request (see Order No. 5689). Due to discrepancies in the vote (and the County’s hearing process) from the August Planning Board meeting, Mr. Royer was allowed by staff to reapply for his variance requests without requiring an application fee, seeking (according to his application):
“Hardship relief on undersize lot, variance relief for pool housing structure: on height roof coverage.”
The Planning and Development Board considered his third variance application at the Board’s September 9, 2025 regular meeting, which again ended in a denial – a 3-3 tie vote on a motion to approve – of his variance requests, which Staff determined at the time to be a denial. Mr. Royer had requested that County staff allow this appeal application to be submitted without an application fee, which was rejected by County staff: this delayed his appeal application submittal.
This second appeal was heard by the Board of County Commissioners at its January 12, 2026 regular meeting. After considering the appeal request, the Board (on a unanimous vote) remanded the appeal back to the Planning and Development Board on the basis that a tie vote is not the basis of denial (as copied below from the Board of County Commissioners Order No. 6024):
“The Board of County Commissioners found that the essential requirements of the law – including primarily the four Criteria for Variances within the LDC – have been observed by the Planning and Development Board. However, the Board’s denial of the application request – due to the tie vote – necessitates the Board’s reconsideration of the variance application for reconsideration of the variance request inclusive of the increase in height of the pump house accessory structure to 9 feet, 7 inches, finding the request meets the criteria for approval of variance under the LDC.”
The application was reheard at the April 14, 2026 Planning and Development Board regular meeting (with the delay at the request of the applicant). An initial motion to approve failed 3-3. A subsequent motion to deny failed 3-3. The Board was reminded by Staff that a motion that ends in a tie is not the basis of either an approval or denial, and that a majority vote on a motion was required. Following Board discussion with the Applicant regarding a possible compromise on the request, it was suggested that the Applicant move the structure to the rear of the property in line with the house. A final motion to continue the request to the August 11, 2026 Regular Meeting (vote on the motion was unanimous) stated:
“The Planning and Development Board continues the variance request to give the applicant time to modify the application. Continuing the variance request to the August 11th Planning and Development Board haring [sic] will preserve public notice and provide an opportunity for staff or the applicant to provide additional information.”
By the August 11, 2026 regular meeting, the applicant had not amended his request. The day of the meeting, the applicant provided an Engineering Evaluation Report competed by LAV Engineering, PLLC and dated August 10, 2026. Due to the late submittal, it was not included in the Staff Report or Staff Presentation but was provided to the Board and the Board Secretary for the record. An initial motion to approve failed 3-3. A subsequent motion to deny failed 3-3. Staff reminded the Board that a motion that ends in a tie is not the basis of either an approval or denial, and that per the LDC, they were limited to one continuance which had already been use. A final motion to deny passed by majority vote 4-2 and stated:
“The Planning and Development Board finds that all the variance criteria as listed in the guidelines at Land Development Code Section 3.07.01.E have not been met, that the requested variance is not the minimum relief necessary to alleviate the hardship, and therefore denies Project No. 2025080063 for a 22.34 left (West) street side setback variance from the minimum required 25-foot street side setback and 1.2 percent lot coverage variance from the maximum allowed 35 percent lot coverage for a pump house at 3 Pelican Lane (Parcel No. 23-11-31-5300-00000-0130).”
As a reminder to the Board, the subject parcel lies on the North side of Pelican Lane, East of Mockingbird Lane):
The Board of County Commissioners is the appellate authority following a decision by the Planning and Development Board pursuant to Section 3.07.03.C.1 of the Land Development Code. In turn, the decision of the Board of County Commissioners may ultimately be appealed to the Circuit Court. It is noted that the Board’s denial of Mr. Royer’s original appeal was not further appealed to the Circuit Court.
The appeal must be reviewed based on the record presented at the Planning and Development Board meetings and also argument of the appellant before the County Commission. No new evidence or testimony may be provided. In deciding, the Board of County Commissioners must make three determinations:
-Whether the Planning and Development Board’s decision was supported by competent substantial evidence;
-Whether due process was accorded; and
-Whether the essential requirements of law (primarily, the four Criteria for Variances within the LDC) have been observed.
As a variance request, the necessary detail is provided to the Planning and Development Board through a site plan. Initial site plan requirements for both variances and special exceptions are listed at LDC Section 3.07.03.A.2. The Planning and Development Board considered the applicants’ site plans, which are included in the back up material attached hereto. It is noted that the day of the August 11, 2026 Planning and Development Board meeting, the applicant provided an Engineering Evaluation Report competed by LAV Engineering, PLLC and dated August 10, 2026.
Specific to variances, the LDC requires (at LDC Sec. 3.07.03.E.) demonstration that the four variance guidelines are considered by a variance applicant, with these guidelines typically depicted on a site plan and through a written narrative (and where “the board [Planning and Development Board] shall be guided by the following”):
“Variance guidelines. A variance may be granted from the terms and provisions of this article where, owing to special conditions relating to the property, a literal enforcement of the provisions of this article will, in an individual case, result in unnecessary hardship. Variances may be granted by the Planning and Development Board in such an individual case of unnecessary hardship upon a written finding based on competent, substantial evidence in the official record that:
1. There are extraordinary and exceptional conditions pertaining to the particular piece of property in question because of its size, shape, topography, or other unique features that, when considered in whole or in part, creates an unnecessary hardship; and
2. Such conditions were not created by the affirmative actions of the applicant and the applicant has acted at all times in good faith; and
3. The variance, if granted, would not cause substantial detriment to the public health, welfare, safety, and morals of the community or impair the purpose and intent of this article; and
4. No variance may be granted for a use of land or building that is not permitted by this article.
A variance, if granted, shall be the minimum variance necessary to alleviate the hardship. For purposes of this section, an unnecessary hardship shall mean that without the granting of the variance the owner will be deprived of all reasonable use of the property as allowed in the zoning district.”
The Planning and Development Board’s findings regarding these criteria are stated in the Planning Board’s Order regarding the variance and are reflected in the Planning Board’s technical staff report attached to this report.
It is assumed that the Appellants’ appeal request claims that the four (4) foot-height limitation originally imposed on the pump house (through the original variance approval) deprives him of his use of the pump house in the intended manner. However, the final paragraph of the Variance guidelines listed above states, “A variance, if granted, shall be the minimum variance necessary to alleviate the hardship.” (Emphasis added). The Planning and Development Board’s intent with the imposed condition was to ensure that the granted variances were the minimum variances necessary to alleviate the hardship, providing space for a pump house but arguably not for housing pool furniture.
This appeal iteration alleges that the “Owners will be deprived of all reasonable use of the property as allowed in the zoning district.” Staff counters that the Planning Board’s decision – a denial preceded with two tie-votes – was indicative of the difficulty posed by his request, where the Planning Board seeks to balance reasonable requests for relief from the strict application of the Land Development Code’s requirements with limitations that respect the adjacent neighborhood and uphold the Code’s intent to protect the health, safety, and general welfare. In staff’s opinion, the Planning Board correctly weighed the evidence and testimony provided in the variance application and at the public hearing and, ultimately, came to a majority consensus resulting in denial. Additionally, the deprivation of “all reasonable use” is not the end result. The previously granted variances – inclusive of the pump house height limitation – provided for the proposed pool development. In the end, the “reasonable use” was not deprived, but instead it was conditioned on a requirement to limit the pump house height. The appeal goes on to state that: “TRC, has stated height is 12’.” This is correct, but the Planning Board opted to restrict the pump house height to less than 12 feet as a condition of granting the requested variances. This is the Board’s prerogative: if the pump house can be placed on the parcel without the variances, then the 12-foot height applies. The appeal now appears to seek a 10’ pump house height, providing a buffer for the previously intended 9’ 7” height: “My application has always maintain [sic] the request of 10’ and the building plans are to build 9’ 7” height with 5” buffer not to exceed 10’.” The Board heard this proposal, and the vote – effectively considered at two separate consecutive meetings – resulted in a majority vote for a denial at the final Planning and Development Board meeting.

description:
Due to recent developments, our current County Administrator search process is left with no active applicants under review. The Board has three possible options to discuss:
Review the current pool of qualified applicants and identify potential candidates to interview, allowing the current selection process to continue.
Pause the current selection process until after the November elections.
Engage an executive recruiting firm and begin a new formal recruitment process.
Each of these options has strengths and weaknesses. Working from the current applicant pool is the quickest (and cheapest) option to pursue, although qualified applicants may have dropped off due to the elapsed time from their initial application and because of previous short-listing of other applicants. Pausing the process until after November delays the selection until after the new Board is seated, and the outcome of Amendment 3 is known. Following the November election, there is likely to be a larger applicant pool due to newly-elected officials and the manager/administrator moves that often coincide with the election cycle. Initiating a new search after November -- more than likely after the New Year -- could then be done with in-house resources or utilizing an executive search firm. Overall, utilizing an executive search firm would be the longest time-wise and most costly of options. With an anticipated cost falling below the County Administrator's $100,000 approval authority, our purchasing policies would allow for County Procurement and HR staff to obtain three quotes and move forward with selection of a search firm without additional review by the Board.
