As the Board is aware, the City of Bunnell's Planning, Zoning and Appeals Board (PZA) approved (3-1) a Special Exception in the AG&S District for a Class I Landfill on 610 acres known as "Project Butterfly." The public -- and the County -- were kept unaware of the project's location and other pertinent details until the day before the PZA meeting when the City staff amended the PZA agenda and backup to reflect the project's location and intended use. Project details were kept confidential by City staff under a Florida Statute that maintains confidentiality of an economic development prospect up until its public review for development, incentive package, tax abatement, or similar approval process before a local governing board.
Following the PZA's approval, County staff have reviewed the County's and the City's respective Comprehensive Plans and land development regulations for consistency of the proposed landfill project. As is the standard, there is text within both the County's and the City's Comprehensive Plan that requires coordination of potentially incompatible land uses. While County staff was involved in a review of concurrency-related issues from the proposed development (which was completed under the terms of the confidentiality agreement between the City and the applicant), a vetting as to incompatibility of the proposed landfill location was not completed.
Pursuant to Section 2-86, Bunnell Code, a decision of the PZA Board may be appealed to the City Commission by filing a written request for such an appeal with the City Clerk. The request must be filed within thirty (30) days of the decision. The PZA Board met and decided this matter on 9/1/2026.
The County Attorney has advised the Board of recommended next steps -- if the Board wishes to pursue a challenge to the City PZA's approval -- beginning with an appeal of the PZA's decision to the Bunnell City Commission. If the City Commission ultimately affirms the PZA's decision approving the landfill, the County Commission could then direct staff to pursue dispute resolution through Chapter 164, Florida Statutes, in much the same manner as was initiated in our dispute with the City of Flagler Beach over the City's approval of Veranda Bay's Comprehensive Plan amendment.
Attachments to this workshop agenda item include: the County's Attorney's email; a copy of Chapter 164, Florida Statutes; relevant excerpts from the County's Comprehensive Plan and Land Development Code; excerpts from the City of Bunnell's Comprehensive Plan and Land Development Code; and (for reference) FDEP's checklist for landfill permitting.

description:
As part of this year's budget review, staff initiated the closure of the County's Household Hazardous Waste dropoff site at 1700 South Old Kings Road. On the 60+/- acre parcel are four buildings: a 1990 office trailer (672 square feet), a 2005 enclosed warehouse (896 square feet), a 1995 metal pole barn (3,154 square feet); and a 1995 metal pole barn (4,850 square feet):
The drop off site is the former landfill site, which closed in 2006:
On August 24, the County announced that the Household Hazardous Waste site would close on September 18. The September 18 date was selected to allow sufficient time for staff at the site to wind-down operations on or before September 30 to coincide with the end of the 2025-26 fiscal year. Through the County's contract with WastePro, household hazardous waste items can be disposed of at the WastePro site at 401 S. Bay Street Bunnell for a nominal fee: "Residents may bring up to 100 pounds or 10 gallons of material, per visit for $25 – apart from tires ($10 for passenger vehicle tires and $25 for commercial and heavy-duty vehicle tires). Residents are asked to call ahead of making drop off, 386-586-0800." Contrary to public opinion on the closure, the operation of the Household Hazardous Waste drop off site is not free of cost: while it may be free of charge for residents to drop off residential hazardous wastes, it comes at considerable cost to the County, which is subsidizing the site's operation for the benefit of all County residents without any municipal cost-share in place. Further, as is the case with most things these days, the County is facing increased costs of operations at the drop off site, chief among these being an upcoming capital expense to replace the office trailer and the primary collection building, both of which have become safety hazards for the County staff working at the site and the public visiting the site. The initial capital expense is estimated at $300,000, while continuing operational expenses include approximately $200,000 annually in payroll and approximately $100,000 in annual hauling and disposal charges (increased this year because of the site's closure: see Consent Agenda Item 7.m. on tonight's regular meeting agenda for a budget transfer to offset the increased volume).
The County utilizes five separate vendors to dispose of these wastes, each specific to a separate waste product: Clean Earth of Alabama (now known as Veolia) disposes of all hazardous wastes; Howco handles all used oil, oil filters, engine coolant, gasoline, as well as any oily debris; Sensible Recycling handles all electronic waste; John's Famous Auto Parts is takes away all lead acid batteries (PB) and certain metals (this is the only material that generates revenue); and WastePro handles any solid waste, scrap metal, waste tires, and cardboard.
Due to the characteristics of these materials, the risk of a spill or accidental discharge, the physical space that is needed for routing and traffic control, and the historic use of the present site as the drop off site, County staff encourages that any future household hazardous waste collection "amnesty" day events be limited to the Old Kings Road site and not be held elsewhere within the county. Collection day events would cost the County an estimated $30,000 to $50,000 per daily event, depending on the amount of material that is dropped off for disposal. The County would realize a savings over the present operation for two or three collection days, depending on the amount of materials received. For four or more collection days, it would make more sense for the County to reopen the drop off site, even when facing increased capital and operating costs.
It should be noted that the City of Bunnell staff have contacted the County regarding the lack of prior notice regarding the County's closure of the Old Kings Road site and the switch to the fee-based WastePro site in Bunnell. According to Bunnell staff, the WastePro site is not appropriately zoned for this use despite its utilization for the duration of WastePro's ownership of this parcel since 2006. As Bunnell staff have mentioned, a Special Exception would be required prior to initiating this use on the WastePro parcel. Any resolution of this would involve the City as the local government having regulatory authority over the WastePro parcel and WastePro as the parcel owner: the County is at best a contracted customer of WastePro.
Should the Board ultimately decide to continue operation of the Household Hazardous Waste drop off site, a budget amendment will be needed to restore funding to the Solid Waste Landfill Fund (1402). Similarly, future collection days will need to be funded through the General Fund.
title: Household Hazardous Waste

description:
Flagler County has been under a declared state of local emergency due to Hurricane Matthew since October 4, 2016. During that time, other storms have struck the County exacerbating the damage to the dune system and compounding the exposure of public and private property on the barrier island to future storms and flooding. The County also declared local states of emergency for Hurricane Irma (2017), Hurricane Dorian (2019), Hurricane Isaias (2020), and Hurricanes Ian and Nicole (2022).
Due to the cumulative effect of the storms as well as tidal events, nor’easters, and erosion, Flagler County continues to be in the most precarious position relative to ocean flooding and storms in its history. Although the County has completed a series of emergency protective berm projects since Hurricane Matthew, public and private property on the barrier island remain vulnerable to catastrophic storm damage without further and sustained protective efforts.
As part of addressing the emergency, the Board adopted a long-term beach management plan assisted by an independent coastal engineer, the County’s engineering staff and with input from residents and local HOAs. Continuing the state of local emergency will help the County with its ongoing and future efforts and allow the County to take any necessary emergency measures, including expedited emergency procurement and the issuance of emergency administrative orders, as necessary.

description:
Flagler County Fire Rescue (FCFR) responds to an average of 410 fire alarm activations per year, of which approximately 90% (369 annually) are confirmed nuisance alarms where no fire or hazardous condition exists. This creates a substantial and growing operational burden, totaling 307 apparatus hours lost each year and an estimated $184,500 in annual taxpayer cost.
The proposed Nuisance Fire Alarm Reduction Program (NFARP) establishes a structured, legally supported approach to reduce false alarms by focusing on public education, registration of monitored systems, enforcement of maintenance requirements, and a tiered fee schedule for repeat offenders. Data demonstrates concentrated nuisance alarm activity in a small number of occupancies, including one specific property, responsible for 248 nuisance alarm responses over three years (20% of all FCFR alarm calls).
The implementation of NFARP will directly improve firefighter safety, increase unit availability for true emergencies, reduce unnecessary budget impacts, and strengthen code compliance across commercial, residential, and high-risk occupancies.
Operational Impact
Nuisance alarms lead to:
• Significant diversion of emergency resources
• Increased risk during emergency vehicle response
• Delayed response times for actual emergencies
• Accelerated wear on apparatus and equipment
• Unnecessary disruption to residents, businesses, and roadways
Each fire alarm response costs approximately $450, consuming 45 minutes of apparatus time on average, aligning with national and local data.
Historical Call Volume Trends
Between 2023–2025, alarm responses increased from 384 to 433 annually, reflecting a 12.8% upward trend. FCFR averages one false alarm every day.
LEGAL AUTHORITY
The program is fully enabled under existing state and national codes:
• F.S. §633.118 – Fire Chief enforcement authority
• F.S. §633.208 – County obligation to enforce the Florida Fire Prevention Code
• FAC 69A-3 & 69A-60 – State Fire Marshal rules
• NFPA 72 – Alarm inspection, testing, and maintenance standards
• NFPA 1 – Fire Code occupancy requirements
• Florida Constitution Art. VIII §1 – County home rule authority
These statutory authorities explicitly designate the Fire Chief as the Authority Having Jurisdiction (AHJ). Implementation of NFARP is consistent with mandated county enforcement responsibilities.
PROGRAM ELEMENTS
Phase 1 – Public Education (First 6 Months)
• County-wide notification effort
• Outreach to alarm contractors and monitoring companies
• Distribution of Fire Alarm System Owner Training Guide to commercial entities
Phase 2 – Mandatory System Registration (Second 6 Months)
• Registration required for all monitored commercial systems
• Initial fee: $25; annual renewal: $15; failure to register: $100 penalty
• Ensures up-to-date contact and contractor information for each property
Phase 3 – Enforcement and Fee Schedule Activation
Once registration and education periods conclude, fees are assessed based on a rolling 12 month period:
Commercial Occupancies
• 1st: Warning
• 2nd: $100
• 3rd: $250
• 4th: $500
• 5th: $750
• 6th+: $1,000 each
Residential Occupancies
• 1st–2nd: Warning
• 3rd: $50
• 4th: $100
• 5th: $250
• 6th+: $500
High-risk occupancies follow an enhanced schedule
Appeals & Exemptions
Property owners may appeal fees within 30 calendar days, supported by contractor reports or monitoring logs. Exemptions apply to:
• Confirmed fires or hazards
• Natural disasters
• Utility failures
• Criminal acts (e.g., malicious activation)
RATIONALE FOR ADOPTION
1. Firefighter & Public Safety
Emergency vehicle operations remain one of the leading causes of firefighter injuries and fatalities. Reducing 369 unnecessary responses annually significantly lowers risk exposure.
2. Improved Response Availability
By eliminating hundreds of nuisance responses, FCFR improves availability for structure fires, EMS calls, vehicle crashes, and other critical incidents.
3. Fiscal Responsibility
The community currently absorbs $184,500/year in avoidable false-alarm costs. NFARP provides a fair, legally defensible method of reducing this burden and recapturing costs from chronic offenders.
4. Regulatory Compliance & Modernization
NFARP aligns Flagler County with national best practices and NFPA 72 requirements for maintenance and modernization of alarm systems.
5. Community Education & Prevention
Property owners receive clear, actionable guidance on how to prevent nuisance alarms—reducing both fees and operational burdens.
title: Consideration of a Nuisance Fire Alarm Reduction Program.

description:
During the July 13, 2026 meeting, the Board provided staff with consensus to issue a Request for Proposals (RFP) for the operation of the David I. Siegel Adult Day Care Center (ADC) program. This was new direction in follow up to the January 12, 2026 workshop, wherein the Board provided staff with consensus to dissolve the Adult Day Care program by the end of this fiscal year on September 30, 2026. Reasons cited by the Board for the dissolution of the program were limited enrollment relative to the ongoing costs of the program, with staff noting that despite the program costs and the equivalent of the County’s subsidy of the program, the program remains significantly less expensive to the enrollee than in-home care.
Subsequently, the Commission received two public-private partnerships requests (pursuant to Sec. 255.065, Florida Statutes) to continue Adult Day Care operations. The board directed staff to issue the RFP in light of this interest. Procurement staff issued 26-RFP-022: Operation and Program Administration of the Flagler County Adult Day Care at the David I. Siegel Center on August 3, 2026, with a proposal closing date of August 24, 2026. Three interested applicants completed the mandatory bidder conference meeting and submitted eligible proposals. Applications were received from Calvin’s Care LLC; Mishpakha Inc.; and Therapeutic Assisted Living Corp.
The evaluation committee met on September 2, 2026 to rank the scored applications, with Therapeutic Assisted Living Corp. as the highest scoring bidder to move forward for Board consideration to operate the ADC. Staff will note that while the vendor ranked highest, there are nuanced differences in the program model, levels of service and related aspects from the bidder, as well as need to ramp up staffing, transition program licensure and other aspects that will take time to complete and ultimately may result in a slightly different program model than when operated by the County. This includes limited RN/LPN staffing, which is allowable under basic ADC state licensure, but may impact medical aspects of the program, such as regular medication management and levels of available medical response in an emergency.
Should the Board approve the highest scoring applicant, staff will work closely and quickly with the vendor to complete a Change of Ownership (CHOW) with the State of Florida Agency for Health Care Administration (AHCA). The CHOW process can take 60-90 days and successful completion is required for transfer of operations. If the selected applicant CHOW is not approved by AHCA, the program licensure and operations cannot be transferred. County staff will also work with the vendor to transfer Medicaid Managed Long Term Care (MLTC) contracts and patients, as well as private pay patient care over to the new vendor. Additionally, the County will complete related agreements with the vendor to memorialize logistical aspects such as facility use and other components.
To enact this measure staff will need to extend the Adult Day Care program between 60-90 days to allow the full transition of licensure ownership and also continuity of care. Three months of gap funding, spanning October 1 to December 31, 2026 have been included in the FY 2026-27 budget to account for this transition time.
One final item of note: ITT has recently released its original deed conditions and restrictions over the subject parcel. This release would allow the County to pursue additional uses of this parcel other than for provision of senior services, or alternatively would allow for the parcel to be disposed of as surplus to the highest and best bidder for redevelopment.
title: Consideration of Approval of Awarding Request for Proposals (RFP) Response from Therapeutic Assisted Living and Carry Out Operational Transition of the David I. Siegel Adult Day Care Center.

This request is for a Future Land Use Map amendment for Parcel Numbers 28-12-31-0000-01010-0000 and 29-12-31-0000-01010-0000. On August 22, 2025, the applicant submitted an application to amend the Future Land Use designation for a total of 119+/- acres across both parcels. The proposed Future Land Use Map amendment will change the present Future Land Use designations from 108+/- acres of Agriculture and Timberlands and 11+/- acres of Commercial Low Intensity to 119+/- of Mixed-Use High Intensity with a Parcel Limiting Policy that reduces the maximum allowed density from ten (10) units per acre to seven (7) units per acre. Following comments made at the June 15, 2026 Board of County Commissioners Transmittal Hearing, in addition to comments received from Florida Commerce, the applicant is revising the parcel limiting policy to also limit the Floor Area Ration (FAR) from 0.4 to 0.2 to be consistent with the proposed PUD Development Agreement. The applicant has proposed that 71.44 acres will be allocated for residential and 47.62 acres will be allocated for commercial yielding a maximum total of 502 dwelling units and a maximum of 414,865 square feet of commercial floor area.
The Mixed-Use High Intensity designation is necessary because the Applicant is seeking inclusion of typical commercial high intensity uses – those permitted in the C-2 (General Commercial and Shopping Center) zoning district – within the proposed PUD (Planned Unit Development). Like the Cornerstone project, the proposed PUD lists the entirety of the C-2 District’s PUD uses within the PUD’s list of permitted uses, excepting Bars, Bowling Alleys, and Laundry and Dry Cleaning Facilities. As stated at the Planning and Development Board hearing, the applicant’s intent is to include a grocery store within a strip commercial center on the commercial portion of the project.
This application is succeeded by an application to rezone the subject parcel from the AC (Agriculture) District to the PUD (Planned Unit Development) District (Project No. 2025080074).
At its February 10, 2026, regular meeting, the Planning and Development Board unanimously recommended approval of the Future Land Use amendment request. The Board of County Commissioners voted 4-1 to approve the amendment on first reading on June 15, 2026, and transmitted the amendment to state agencies for review and comment.
While none of the reviewing agencies had any comments requiring changes less they became the basis of a challenge, both FloridaCommerce, the state land planning agency, and the Florida Department of Transportation provided technical comments/ recommendations.
FloridaCommerce provided technical comments related to scrivener’s errors (that have since been corrected), public facility impact mitigation by the applicant, addition of the proposed FAR of 0.2 (down from 0.4) to the parcel limiting policy, and consideration to submit under the State Coordinated Review Process.
The applicant has provided in their response to agency comments letter, provided as attachment 8, that they agree to limit the FAR to 0.2 by revising the parcel limiting policy, that the revised PUD agreement addresses public facilities on a phase-by-phase basis and requires the necessary infrastructure and services to be available as development proceeds.
The Florida Department of Transportation provided two recommendations: to correct a scrivener’s error and to request the County coordinate with FDOT in reviewing final traffic analysis at the site development approval stage.
In its response letter, the applicant has provided that future development will remain subject to transportation concurrency and any additional traffic analysis required at the plat or site-plan stage.
Based on the comments, staff and the applicant assert that the agencies' technical comments and recommendation can be satisfactorily addressed and the amendment is appropriate for the Board’s consideration at this time.

description:
This request is for rezoning for the Seminole Woods Mixed Use PUD – from the AC (Agriculture) District to the PUD (Planned Unit Development) District – for a mixed-use development to be developed in multiple phases. The subject project area is 119+/- acres in size and is located on the North side of Seminole Woods Blvd:
On August 26, 2025, the applicant submitted an application to rezone the subject parcel to establish the Seminole Woods Mixed Use PUD. The project is accessed from Seminole Woods Boulevard.
The Seminole Woods Mixed Use PUD requires a Future Land Use Map amendment from Ag and Timber and Commercial Low Intensity to Mixed-Used: High Intensity. The applicant has also proposed a parcel-limiting policy to lower the density from 10 units per acre allowed under Mixed-Use High Intensity to 7 units per acre. Following comments from the Board of County Commissioners during the first reading at the June 15, 2026 regular meeting, and from FloridaCommerce, the applicant is proposing to revise the parcel limiting policy to also limit the FAR (Floor Area Ratio) from 0.4 to 0.2. The pending rezoning request, from AC (Agriculture) to PUD (Planned Unit Development), will ultimately be conditioned upon the companion Future Land Use Map amendment (Project No. 2025080074) becoming effective for the subject parcel.
This application was reviewed by the Technical Review Committee (TRC) at its September 17, 2025, and November 19, 2025, regular meetings. The applicant has satisfactorily addressed the TRC comments.
This application was considered at the December 9, 2025 Planning and Development Board regular meeting. Following questions by the Board, the Board voted to continue the request to the January 13, 2026 Planning and Development Board regular meeting. However, the meeting date had to be rescheduled to January 8, 2026, and the application was re-noticed according to Section 125.66, Florida Statutes, and Land Development Code (LDC) Section 2.07.00. The January 8, 2026 Planning and Development Board Meeting was canceled due to a lack of quorum of the Board. The application was then re-noticed for the February 10, 2026 Planning and Development Board regular meeting according to Section 125.66, Florida Statutes, and Land Development Code (LDC) Section 2.07.00.
The Board continuation was based on the question of whether the City of Palm Coast had any comments on the potential transportation impacts of the project on Seminole Woods Boulevard. City of Palm Coast staff provided their comments on January 22, 2026, at which time they stated that there is adequate capacity to accommodate the proposed traffic impacts. The City’s comments are attached to this report.
The Planning and Development Board considered this request at its February 10, 2026 regular meeting. Public comments were provided under the companion Future Land Use amendment application. For the most part, public comments objected to the inclusion of shopping centers and related uses within the list of permitted uses allowed within the PUD. Most of the residents were new to Palm Coast (within the last 5-10 years) and were unaware of ITT’s Comprehensive Land Use Plan (CLUP), which was described as part of Michael Chiumento’s presentation to the Board. The CLUP designated a Neighborhood Scale Village Center proximate to the subject parcel. The CLUP – as described by Mr. Chiumento – included an estimated population of 225,000 at full buildout of Palm Coast. The Board unanimously recommended approval of the request.
This request was originally noticed for the March 16, 2026 Board of County Commissioners regular meeting. The applicant requested the item be continued to the June 15, 2026 regular meeting. This continuance was noted on the March 16, 2026 regular meeting agenda and thus public notice was preserved.
Between the February 10, 2026 Planning and Development Board meeting and the first reading at the June 15, 2026 Board of County Commissioner meeting, the applicant modified the request to include more restrictive requirements in the proposed development agreement attached as Exhibit 1. These more restrictive requirements included reducing the maximum allowed Floor Area Ratio (FAR) from 0.4 to 0.2, which reduces the maximum allowed total Floor Area from 829,382 square feet to 414,691 square feet. The applicant also removed Bars, Bowling Alleys, and Laundry and Dry-Cleaning facilities from the list of permitted uses. Finally, the applicant added additional language pertaining to landscape buffers. Any commercial or multifamily uses located along the northern property line will require a 25-foot buffer where it abuts existing residentially-developed properties; otherwise, the buffer standards shall be in accordance with the Flagler County Land Development Code.
Since the first reading of the request at the June 15, 2026 Board of County Commissioners meeting, the applicant has modified the request in response to comments made during the hearing in addition to revising the parcel limiting policy to reduce the FAR from 0.4 to 0.2 as part of the Future Land Use Amendment. The revisions are intended to clarify the language and establish objective standards for future review. A more detailed summary of the changes can be found in the Cover Letter included in this report as Attachment 3. A brief summary is provided below:
Sec 2.1 and 3.0 – Clarifies that the Master Plan is conceptual and subject to change, but will not add new uses or increase the density or intensity authorized by the agreement.
Sec. 2.2 – Clarifies that staff may approve only minor modifications that do not add a new use(s) or increase density or intensity; otherwise, a PUD amendment is required.
Sec. 3.0 and 4.2 – In direct response to concerns regarding impacts on existing residential properties, the Agreement now establishes designated Viewshed Protection Zones adjacent to existing residential development. These areas cannot be relocated, reduced, or modified without approval of the Board of County Commissioners.
Sec 2.3 – Clarifies that the PUD does not lapse due to a delay or phased approach to development.
Sec 2.4 – Clarifies that each phase must independently address access, utilities, stormwater and applicable development approvals.
Sec 3.1 – Clarifies that mixed-use buildings or development pods are permitted.
Sec 4.0 – Clarifies that the overall project has an FAR of 0.2.
Sec 4.3 – Adds language that expressly requires compliance with SJRWMD requirements, specifies design standards for stormwater conveyance and detention, addresses FEMA flood-zone procedures, and requires residential finished-floor elevations at or above the FEMA 100-year floodplain elevation
Sec 4.6 – Clarifies that the development has an overall open space requirement of 25 percent.
Sec 4.10 – Adds language that the project is subject to the County’s Land Development Code and Comprehensive Plan, unless preempted by state or federal regulations.
Sec 5.1 – Adds language that the County retains the ability to require updated traffic analysis at future plat and site-plan stages when required by the LDC.
The Board’s ultimate approval of the PUD will be contingent on the approval of the prerequisite Future Land Use amendment.

In 1980, the Florida Legislature adopted what is known as the Truth-in-Millage Legislation also known as TRIM. The goal of the legislation is to ensure that taxpayers are advised of the public hearings at which the local taxing authorities' budgets and millage rates are considered and adopted. Each year, the Property Appraiser completes an assessment of the value of all property and certifies to each taxing authority the taxable value of the property within its jurisdiction. Each taxing authority then notifies the Property Appraiser of its proposed millage rate, its rolled back rate and the date, time and place of the public hearing to consider the proposed millage rate and the tentative budget. Once the Property Appraiser receives the information, he sends a notice that includes all the referenced information by first class mail to every taxpayer on the assessment role. The notice sent to taxpayers is called the TRIM notice. The TRIM notice lists what the taxes were for the prior year, what the taxes will be if the proposed budget changes are made, and what the taxes will be if no budget changes are made. This information is listed for each taxing authority. The notice also lists all voted levies for debt service. The purpose of the TRIM notice is to provide taxpayers with sufficient basic information to enable them to participate in the public hearing process.

description:
Flagler County Fire Rescue (FCFR) has incurred unavoidable overtime due to the demands of emergency service staffing. Minimum staffing requirements, personal leave, and a limited number of personnel qualified to fill critical operational roles—such as rescue supervisors, drivers, lieutenants—have all contributed to continued overtime use. When staff in these essential positions take leave, properly trained staff must be brought in on overtime to maintain safe and compliant operations. These challenges are common throughout the fire service, making some overtime necessary to maintain full operational readiness.
Another factor affecting the FCFR budget is the timing of the collective bargaining agreement, which was finalized after the budget was set. The agreement included a transition to a 52-hour workweek that began three months earlier than planned. While this early implementation supported long-term staffing goals, it also resulted in an unanticipated increase in salary and overtime costs. FCFR’s overtime budget was reduced by $300,000 in FY 2025-26 due to the anticipation of savings associated with the 52-hour workweek, but the early implementation resulted in additional overtime costs. FCFR has now successfully met all operational staffing requirements for the 52‑hour schedule.
The transition to the 52-hour week was driven in part by House Bill 929 (2025) which ultimately became state law under Florida Statute 633.508(7). HB 929 was passed by the Florida legislature in an effort to improve firefighter mental health and wellness. Ultimately, this legislation encourages local governments to move toward implementation of a 42-hour workweek for firefighters and paramedics encouraging a reduction in on-the-job injuries, fatalities, and occupational diseases.
FCFR was also requested by the State of Florida to provide mutual aid support for wildfires in Putnam and Clay counties under the State Mutual Aid agreement and has submitted a reimbursement request in the amount of $45,133.
Fire Rescue remains committed to reducing overtime where feasible, without compromising service levels. The department has also canceled planned purchases and reduced operating expenditure to redirect funds toward personnel needs. These efforts will continue throughout the remainder of the fiscal year.
title: Approval of Budget Transfer from General Fund (1001) Reserves to Offset Fire Rescue Salary and Overtime Expenditures.

description:
The Phoenix Crossings project is a planned garden apartment complex in Bunnell that will serve as an affordable housing project to meet the housing needs of youth aging out of foster care, individuals with disabling conditions, and households with extremely low incomes. The proposed complex consists of 28 units, which will include 12 two-bedroom, one bath units and 16 three-bedroom, two bath units.
The County previously approved subsidizing the cost of constructing four of the proposed units, with $330,000 provided through its 2023/2024 allotment from the State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) program and $170,000 provided through its allotment of American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) funds. The Board reviewed and approved the ARPA funding at its October 7, 2024 meeting, the SHIP funding at its November 18, 2024 meeting, as well as subsequent clarifying amendments on January 12, 2026 and February 9, 2026.
The SHIP funds were awarded recognizing funding requirements contained in the 2023-2025 SHIP Local Housing Assistance Plan (LHAP) relative to Small Rental Development Projects. Among those requirements is the project sponsor must ensure that all SHIP-assisted units are occupied by income-eligible tenants no later than June 30, 2026 to ensure statutory compliance with the SHIP expenditure deadline for the 2023-24 fund year allocation. On March 20, 2026, Abundant Life submitted an extension request to the SHIP Rental Development Agreement and the ARPA Subrecipient Agreement, noting several factors leading to delays in project development and completion that would make it impossible to meet the June 30, 2026 deadline.
At the April 20, 2026 Board of County Commissioners meeting, the Board approved the extension request conditioned upon the ARPA Agreement being amended to include a claw back provision requiring return of the ARPA funds previously reimbursed by the County if building permits are not pulled by September 1, 2026. At that same meeting, the Board also ratified the earlier recorded SHIP Satisfaction of Mortgage and Termination of Declaration of Restrictions, both of which had been recorded prior to the April 20 meeting to assist Phoenix Crossings in securing its main project funding. At its May 18, 2026 meeting, the Board of County Commissioners approved the Assignment and First Amendment to the ARPA Agreement for purposes of including the requested claw back provision.
Now that all conditions precedent have taken place, it is appropriate for the Board of County Commissioners to consider a new SHIP Rental Development Agreement issued in favor of the new project sponsor, Phoenix Crossings, LLC. As with the previous agreement, the replacement agreement provides that the project will be subject to a 30-year affordability period. Four units must be rented to tenants at or below 80% of the area’s median income for the entire term. Units must be constructed and occupied by income-eligible tenants by June 30, 2027. At the conclusion of the 30-year affordability period, all obligations will be discharged and released by the County. So that there is no question relative to the status of the earlier-approved SHIP Rental Development Agreement, the new SHIP Agreement specifically recognizes that the earlier agreement is null and void and has Abundant Life joining in the Agreement for purposes of acknowledging same.
While the County was working with Phoenix Crossings on the new SHIP Rental Development Agreement, the LLC secured its main project financing. Those lenders, Florida Housing Finance Corporation and the Florida Community Loan Fund, have both asked that the County agree to subordinate its mortgage to the senior lenders' mortgages. Accordingly, staff is also asking the Board to approve the subordination agreements presented by the lenders, which subordinate position is recognized in the County's mortgage.

description:
Flagler County Fire Rescue is requesting Board approval to submit an application to the Florida Firefighter Cancer Decontamination Equipment Grant Program, established under Florida Statute 633.137 and F.A.C. 69A‑37.503. This program provides funding to assist fire departments in acquiring equipment designed to reduce firefighter exposure to carcinogens encountered during fireground operations.
This request seeks grant funding for an SCBA/PPE Multi‑Washer and Decontamination Unit, a specialized extractor capable of removing hazardous cancer‑causing contaminants from self-contained breathing apparatus (SCBA) equipment at a level that standard machines cannot achieve.
An SCBA extractor is an essential piece of equipment for any fire department because it ensures that SCBA components are properly cleaned and decontaminated after emergency responses. During fire operations, SCBA masks, harnesses, and regulators are exposed to smoke, carcinogens, chemical residues, and other hazardous contaminants. Without proper cleaning, these substances can accumulate on equipment and pose long-term health risks to firefighters, as well as reduce the reliability and lifespan of the SCBA units. These washer/decontamination units will allow SCBAs to be cleaned at the stations, reduce transport time for the purpose of deconning, minimize the need for temporary gear exchange, and return firefighters to full protective readiness more quickly.
This grant program provides for 75 percent of the equipment cost being provided by the State of Florida and the remaining 25 percent from the applicant (non-state matching funds). The grant performance period runs July 1, 2026 – June 30, 2027. Matching funds in the amount of $12,283 will be utilized from the FY 2027 Fire Rescue budget, and staff will return to the Board for acceptance and appropriation, if awarded.
title: Approval of an Application for a Firefighter Cancer Decon Equipment Grant. Request the Board authorize submission of the application to the Florida Firefighter Cancer Decontamination Equipment Grant Program for acquisition of an SCBA/PPE Multi‑Washer and Decontamination Unit.

description:
Self Contained Breathing Apparatus (SCBA) units are critical life safety equipment for firefighters, providing respiratory protection in immediately dangerous to life or health (IDLH) environments. To ensure the highest level of safety and reliability, Flagler County Fire Rescue (FCFR) follows nationally recognized standards established by the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA), specifically NFPA 1970: Standard on Protective Ensembles for Structural and Proximity Firefighting, Work Apparel, Open-Circuit Self-Contained Breathing Apparatus (SCBA) for Emergency Services, and Personal Alert Safety Systems (PASS), and NFPA 1850: Standard on Selection, Care, and Maintenance of Protective Ensembles for Structural and Proximity Firefighting and Open-Circuit Self-Contained Breathing Apparatus (SCBA).
NFPA 1850 (2026 edition) the newest, most up-to-date standard governing SCBA selection, care, and maintenance recommends that fire departments develop a comprehensive replacement schedule and identifies ten (10) years as the industry-accepted service life for SCBA components, including the harness, regulator, electronics, and facepieces. NFPA 1850 through its 2026 edition is itself a recent consolidation, merging the former NFPA 1851 (protective ensembles) and NFPA 1852 (open-circuit SCBA) into a single standard.
After ten (10) years of service, SCBA units often reach the end of their certified life due to several factors:
Advancing safety technology: Each revision of the NFPA 1970 standard, the current governing standard for SCBA design and performance, incorporates improved safety requirements, including enhanced thermal performance, accountability electronics, communications, and failure-resistant materials. NFPA 1970 (2025 edition) is also a recent consolidation, combining the former NFPA 1971, 1981, and 1982 standards. Because both governing standards have been substantially rewritten within the past two years, older SCBAs cannot simply be upgraded to meet these newer safety benchmarks — the underlying design and performance requirements have changed too fundamentally for retrofits to bring legacy units into compliance.
Component degradation: SCBAs are exposed to extreme heat, chemical contaminants, moisture, and physical stress. Even with proper maintenance, seals, wiring, plastic housings, sensors, and pressure-bearing components degrade over time, increasing the risk of malfunction.
End of manufacturer support: After the 10-year mark, most manufacturers discontinue parts, software support, and service for older models, making safe maintenance impossible.
Operational reliability requirements: Firefighters depend on SCBA units in environments where equipment failure can be fatal. A structured 10-year replacement ensures all personnel are equipped with reliable, certifiable units that meet the latest NFPA performance and safety requirements.
The current inventory of SCBA within FCFR predates these updated standards and is reaching the 10-year service life, making these due for replacement.
Staff are also seeking Board approval to increase the Ten-8 Cooperative Purchase Agreement 22-730K by $965,486.19. The increase in contract spend will allow the department to purchase the necessary SCBA units. Ten-8 is used for multiple Fire Rescue items, which includes uniforms, fire equipment, supplies, and other services.

description:
On June 18, 2026, Mr. John K. Henley submitted a letter requesting that the Board release the Conservation Easement on Lot 70 in Armand Beach East Subdivision, as recorded in Map Book 8, Pages 21 and 22, Public Records of Flagler County, Florida. Mr. Henley and others have approached the Board over the last twenty years attempting to release the Conservation Easement. This easement is particularly onerous for Lots 70 and 71 due to the easement extending over the entirety of both lots, leaving no lot area outside of the easement.
As best can be determined (although the cause and effect are somewhat in dispute), the Conservation Easement was imposed on Stan Rosenbaum as the successor to the original developer of the Armand Beach East subdivision, Armand Fischetti. Contractors working on behalf of Mr. Rosenbaum had initiated site work without proper permitting or authorization from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, prompting the imposition of the Conservation Easement over portions of the subdivision. This easement was dated February 27, 1992 and was recorded on March 3, 1992 at Official Records Book 462, Page 1370, Public Records of Flagler County, Florida.
The Conservation Easement was accompanied by a list of Restrictions and Covenants to be enforced by the County pursuant to Sec. 704.06, Fla. Stat. Among these restrictions was a prohibition on construction within the easement except on pilings, a prohibition on the placement of soil (except as authorized by USACOE Permit Number 89-IPW-90020), and a prohibition on the removal or destruction of trees or shrubs. Over the years, landowners have developed consistent with the easement’s restrictions, constructing on pilings as needed. Others have cleared into the easement areas prompting Code Enforcement action to restore these areas. Specific to Lots 70 and 71, the Restrictions and Covenants have rendered these lots unbuildable, and for other lots made development complicated.
The Conservation Easement was divided into two parts: part identified as recreated wetlands, within which Mr. Rosenbaum was required to plant Spartina (depicted as a shaded area on the easement’s sketch); and part identified as existing/remaining wetlands (depicted as lined areas on the easement’s sketch). The total area of recreated wetlands was 3.9671 acres, and the area of existing wetlands was 1.9863 acres: total of both areas within the Conservation Easement was 5.9534 acres. The saltwater overwash from Hurricane Matthew ended up filling most of the Spartina that had remained from the Corps’ required planting within the recreated wetland areas. Brazilian Pepper has also encroached into many of these areas.
The sketch was accompanied by a legal description of the Conservation Easement, which described both the recreated and remaining wetlands within six separate areas depicted and described as Parcels A through F:

Of note is the presence of platted 7.5 foot wide drainage and utility easements along all rear and side lot lines, with these easements coinciding with the conservation easements in most of the locations where the conservation easement was imposed. This created a conflict over the years where a drainage easement was located within a conservation easement where a lot owner would be subject to the prohibitive Restrictions and Covenants. As recent as 2024, the County inquired with the HOA about their stance on clearing within the easement, especially where the conservation easement and the platted drainage easement coincided: the HOA replied that they had not and would not override the County to require drainage easement maintenance within a conservation easement where maintenance was otherwise prohibited.
There had been attempts to release the easement in the past, but the Board opted to keep the Conservation Easement in place. The Conservation Easement was intended to be a perpetual easement with no expiration, but there were provisions for transfer and for termination, with termination reverting the use of the land to each respective lot owner:
“In the event Grantee or its successor assigns, abandons, terminates or surrenders the Conservation Easement, the conservation property will revert to the holder of the fee of the conservation property.”
Correspondence to Ms. Wilks and Mr. Henley in 2022 (attached) indicated that, from the County’s standpoint, not much had changed over the years. The physical conditions that required imposition of the Conservation Easement originally remain in place. description:
Flagler County has been under a declared state of local emergency due to Hurricane Matthew since October 4, 2016. During that time, other storms have struck the County exacerbating the damage to the dune system and compounding the exposure of public and private property on the barrier island to future storms and flooding. The County also declared local states of emergency for Hurricane Irma (2017), Hurricane Dorian (2019), Hurricane Isaias (2020), and Hurricanes Ian and Nicole (2022).
Due to the cumulative effect of the storms as well as tidal events, nor’easters, and erosion, Flagler County continues to be in the most precarious position relative to ocean flooding and storms in its history. Although the County has completed a series of emergency protective berm projects since Hurricane Matthew, public and private property on the barrier island remain vulnerable to catastrophic storm damage without further and sustained protective efforts.
As part of addressing the emergency, the Board adopted a long-term beach management plan assisted by an independent coastal engineer, the County’s engineering staff and with input from residents and local HOAs. Continuing the state of local emergency will help the County with its ongoing and future efforts and allow the County to take any necessary emergency measures, including expedited emergency procurement and the issuance of emergency administrative orders, as necessary.

This request is quasi-judicial in nature and requires disclosure of ex parte communication.
The appellant filed an Appeal of a Planning and Development Board Decision application with the County on October 14, 2026. The appeal request is related to the Planning and Development Board’s Denial of a Special Exception for a Restaurant in the R/C (Residential Limited Commercial) District at 5047 N Ocean Shore Blvd at the September 8, 2026 regular meeting.
The Special Exception was unanimously denied by the Board on the basis that all the special exception criteria as listed in the guidelines at Land Development Code Section 3.07.03.F had not been met, and specifically that the provided off-street parking was not adequate. The denial was memorialized through Order No. 6572 dated September 18, 2026 and recorded September 22, 2026 at Official Records Book 3088, Page 729, Public Records of Flagler County.
The intent of the Special Exception application was to, in essence, reinstate an expired Special Exception approval for a Restaurant. The subject property was originally approved for a Special Exception in the R/C District for Restaurant Use in 2018 (Order No. 3122, Official Records Book 2257, Page 1496, Public Records of Flagler County, Florida). The 2018 approval limited the use to a sit down and takeout restaurant only with a maximum of forty seats located outdoors and an onsite brewery. However, the approval was also conditioned to run with the applicant rather than with the land, stating that at such a time as Hammock Enterprises LLC conveyed any portion of its ownership interest in the subject property, the Special Exception would automatically expire.
On January 11, 2019, Hammock Enterprises, LLC conveyed the property to Brent Bruns, Sr. through a Quit Claim Deed (Official Records Book 2329, Page 1556, Official Records of Flagler County, Florida). This conveyance, and therefore expiration of the Special Exception, went unnoticed until Staff was alerted to advertised Special Events occurring on the property. Following research of the approval, Staff alerted the property owner that the Special Exception had expired due to the conveyance of the property. Although the property owner has conveyed the property back to Hammock Enterprises, LLC on April 17, 2026 through a Quit Claim Deed (Official Records Book 3047, Page 1793, Public Records of Flagler County, Florida), the Special Exception remains expired as the conveyance was not sufficient to reinstate it.
In the submitted appeal application, the appellant’s provided basis for appeal discusses the expiration of the 2018 Special Exception:
“Under Florida law, a Special Exception runs with the land and is not extinguished solely by a change in ownership. Accordingly, the Applicant requests reversal of the denial and recognition of the previously approved Special Exception.”
The 2018 Special Exception was specifically conditioned to run with the applicant rather than with the land. Any concerns or questions regarding the 2018 approval and its conditions should have been raised, and an appeal filed, within 30 days of the rendering of Order No. 3122. The deadline to appeal the condition found in the 2018 Special Exception expired on March 30, 2018. No timely appeal of the 2018 approval was ever filed, and no argument relative to the 2018 approval was made at the 2026 Planning and Development Board hearing nor would it have been appropriate to do so.
In the attached cover letter, the appellants, through their agent, also argue that the failure to provide adequate off-street parking in the 2026 Special Exception should not invalidate the previous special exception use:
“Further, the Board's denial specifically cited inadequate off-street parking, notwithstanding that the 2018 Approval expressly authorized restaurant use with a maximum of ten (10) onsite parking spaces. Although the Owner acknowledges that modifications to the proposed restaurant and site improvements may require additional review and permitting, those considerations should not independently invalidate the previously approved restaurant use.”
In making its determination, the Planning and Development Board treated the 2026 request as a new application without giving consideration to the previous 2018 approval. This was because the 2018 approval had expired and, since the earlier approval, the applicant has constructed an abundance of exterior features, much of which was done without permits, with the intent of creating a destination-themed restaurant; cave structures, waterfalls, faux trees, a river/lagoon with bridges, elevated platforms and structures, and an outdoor gastro pub/bar have been added. The special exception request included the use of the property including the additional features as a restaurant, the conversion of the existing single-family residence (constructed in 1959 according to property appraiser records) to a commercial use/commercial kitchen, and the preservation of the existing single-family cottage (constructed in 1940 according to property appraiser records) in the southeast corner of the property for residential use.
The applicant had proposed 10 parking spaces with 1 ADA space and 1 standard space located in front of the building and 8 spaces located in the rear (northeast corner). The LDC provides a parking minimum of 1 space for every 50 square feet of gross seating area and 1 space for each employee on shift. The applicant had provided they would have 3 employees, which leaves 350.77 square feet of seating area available. Due to overall square footage of the project greatly exceeding the maximum seating area allowed by the provided parking, staff proposed a condition on the specific number and type of seating. However, the Planning and Development Board ultimately found this to be an inadequate method to ensure compliance and subsequently denied the request.
The Board of County Commissioners is the appellate authority following a decision by the Planning and Development Board pursuant to Section 3.07.03.C.1 of the Land Development Code. In turn, the decision of the Board of County Commissioners may ultimately be appealed to the Circuit Court.
The appeal must be reviewed based on the record presented at the Planning and Development Board meetings and also argument of the appellant before the County Commission. No new evidence or testimony may be provided. In deciding, the Board of County Commissioners must make three determinations:
1. Whether the Planning and Development Board’s decision was supported by competent substantial evidence;
2. Whether due process was accorded; and
3. Whether the essential requirements of law (primarily, the nine Criteria for Special Exceptions) have been observed.
As a reminder, no credence is to be given to arguments relative to the 2018 approval or its status when considering the current appeal, as the time to appeal the 2018 approval has long since passed. ​
For special exceptions requests, the necessary detail is provided to the Planning and Development Board through a site plan and narrative response. Initial site plan requirements for special exceptions are listed at LDC Section 3.07.03.A.2. Specific to special exceptions, the LDC requires (at LDC Sec. 3.07.03.F.) the applicant to demonstrate that the nine special exception criteria (set forth below) have been considered:
“Special exception guidelines. The planning board shall hear and decide upon requests for special exceptions as authorized by land classifications. The board may approve, with conditions, requests which are in harmony with the intent and purpose of the regulations. In making its determination, the board shall be guided by the following:
1. Ingress to and egress from the property shall provide for automotive and pedestrian safety and convenience, shall not unduly interfere with traffic flow and control, and shall provide access in case of fire or catastrophe.
2. Offstreet parking and loading areas shall be provided as required, shall take into account relevant factors in subsection 1. preceding, and shall be located to minimize economic, noise, glare or odor effects on adjacent and nearby properties.
3. Refuse and service areas shall be located with consideration for relevant factors in subsections 1. and 2. preceding.
4. The proposed use shall be compatible with the availability and location of utility services, whether public or private.
5. Screening and buffering shall be provided which preserves or improves compatibility and harmony of use and structure between the proposed use and adjacent and nearby properties, according to the type, dimensions and character of the proposed use.
6. Signs and exterior lighting, if any, shall maintain traffic safety and minimize glare and economic effects on adjacent and nearby properties.
7. Required yards and open spaces shall be provided.
8. The height of structures shall be in harmony with that of adjacent and nearby uses and structures.
9. The economic effect of the proposed use on adjacent and nearby properties shall be positive.
In granting any special exception, the board may prescribe appropriate conditions and safeguards in conformity with these development regulations. Violation of such conditions and safeguards, when made a part of the terms under which the special exception is recommended, shall be deemed a violation of these development regulations. In granting a special exception, the board shall prescribe a time limit within which the uses for which the special exception, if granted, shall be begun or completed, or both. Failure to begin or complete, or both, such use within the time limit shall void the special exception.”
The Planning and Development Board considered the applicants’ site plan and narrative submittals, which address the criteria referenced above and are included in the back-up material attached hereto. The Board’s findings regarding these criteria are stated in the Planning Board’s Order regarding the special exception and are reflected in the Planning Board’s technical staff reports attached to this report.

The County contracted with Inspire Placemaking Collective, Inc., to update the 2010-2035 Comprehensive Plan to integrate the Comprehensive Plan with relevant elements of the County’s Strategic Plan, along with an update to the Comprehensive Plan to meet statutory changes and best planning practices. Inspire and County staff sought the input of the public, stakeholders, the County’s Planning and Development Board, and the Board of County Commissioners throughout the update process.
The Board of County Commissioners – in its review of the updated Comprehensive Plan – is acting in its capacity as the County’s Local Planning Agency (LPA).
This Comprehensive Plan Update was originally heard at the July 14, 2025 regular meeting and was approved on first reading for transmittal to the State and reviewing agencies. Following transmittal and after discussions with FloridaCommerce, the state land planning agency, staff determined that the update would not be consistent with Senate Bill 180 (Chapter No. 2025-190, Laws of Florida), which prohibits the adoption of more burdensome regulations. As such, the transmittal was withdrawn on August 8, 2025.
Over the past year, numerous jurisdictions have challenged the state land planning agency’s authority to determine what is ‘more burdensome’ and have had their comprehensive plan updates both transmitted and adopted. Following this pattern of successful plan transmittals and adoptions, a re-transmittal of Flagler County’s Comprehensive Plan Update was heard at the July 13, 2026 regular meeting and was approved.
The Flagler County Comprehensive Plan Update was transmitted to FloridaCommerce and the reviewing state agencies as an amendment based on an Evaluation and Appraisal of the Comprehensive Plan (EAR) through the State Coordinated Review Process on July 21, 2026.
The state land planning agency and the reviewing agencies, specifically FloridaCommerce, FDOT, and FDEP, provided their comments on September 21, 2026. The FWC, SJRWMD, and the NEFRC provided that they had no comments.
FloridaCommerce provided two Objections that could be the basis of a challenge. The first was to update the Data and Analysis to reflect the required short-term 10-year Planning Horizon. The Data and Analysis was originally based on the year 2025 (the intended year of adoption) and thus reflected the years 2035, 2045 and 2050. To address the comment, the Data and Analysis has been updated to reflect the year 2036.
The second objection was to ensure the Level of Service (LOS) standard for transportation was consistent between the Transportation Element and Capital Improvements Element, and to ensure that policies that reference external elements, codes, or specific standards provide sources so the policies are meaningful and predictable. These have been revised to address the objection.
FloridaCommerce also provided a technical comment to address the following FDOT and FDEP Comments.
The Florida Department of Transportation provided recommendations to revise and correct the data within the tables of the Data and Analysis of the Transportation Element. These have been revised.
The Florida Department of Environmental Protection provided two technical comments. The first states that the County must include a list of projects necessary to achieve pollutant load reduction attributable to County in the Lower St. John’s Basin Management Action Plan (BMAP) per s.163.3177(3)(a)4.b, F.S. However, according to the 2025 Lower St. Johns BMAP, on page 30, there are no pollutant load reductions attributable to the County.
The second technical comment states the County must consider the feasibility of providing sanitary sewer services to developments with a density of more than one unit per acre per s. 163.3177(6)(c)3, F.S. However, Section 2.2.1. of the Data and Analysis for the Infrastructure Element states the “County does not operate a wastewater treatment plant or collection system, and has no ability to assess the feasibility of converting septic system in the unincorporated area. However, the County will continue supporting efforts to secure funding that facilitates septic-to-sewer conversions in coordination with municipal and private utility providers.”
In addition to the formal Objections and Technical Comments, FloridaCommerce has also provided a list of policies that it has determined may be more burdensome in conflict with SB180. A summary of these identified policies is attached. FloridaCommerce has issued Notices of Intent to find the comprehensive plan amendments “In Compliance” despite identifying more burdensome policies; for example, the City of Debary received a ‘Notice of Intent’ to find the City’s comprehensive plan update in compliance despite the identification of more burdensome policies.
Approval of the update to the Comprehensive Plan at this stage will submit the adopted update to the state land planning agency and reviewing agencies that provided comments as an amendment based on an Evaluation and Appraisal of the Comprehensive Plan (EAR) through the State Coordinated Review Process. If no challenges are filed, the update will become effective when the state land planning agency issues a Notice of Intent to find the Comprehensive Plan Update In Compliance within 45 days of submittal.

description:
The purpose of this public hearing is to consider the adoption of a resolution notifying the public of the County's intent to use the uniform ad valorem method for collecting a non-ad valorem assessment levied by the Flagler County Board of County Commissioners for the fiscal year commencing October 1, 2027, and continuing from year to year thereafter. The assessment will fund fire rescue services, facilities, and programs in the unincorporated area of the County and within the incorporated areas of Bunnell, Beverly Beach, and Marineland.
No assessment is levied by adoption of this resolution. This resolution is the first step in notifying the public of the County's intent to use the ad valorem tax bill to collect the non-ad valorem assessment and is required by Section 197,3632, Florida Statutes. The County has hired a consultant to determine the special benefit received by the property owners subject to the assessment as well as the fair method of apportioning the assessment among the property owners.
Each property owner within the benefit unit will receive mailed notice of the amount of the assessment along with the date and time at which the County Commission would hold a public hearing to levy it, which must be held prior to September 15, 2027. The city commissions of Bunnell, Beverly Beach, and Flagler Beach must consent to the levy on properties within their respective jurisdictions. The County will also need to enter interlocal agreements with the Property Appraiser and Tax Collector to compensate those offices for administering the assessment.
